items.descriptionOriginal: "Education can become a burden when a family has limited resources." For Paturi Namratha Siri, a student from Yernagudem village in Andhra Pradesh, there were times when continuing her education felt difficult . She did not always have the learning resources or support she needed after school. "Understanding some subjects was hard, and I needed additional guidance," she explains. Her experience is familiar to Bethala Veera Swami, who is now 58 years old and grew up in the same village several decades earlier. The village he remembers Born in 1968, he spent his childhood in Yernagudem, studying from Class 1 to Class 10. His parents were daily-wage agricultural labourers. The family had a small piece of land, but it was not enough to provide for everyone through the year. "My father and mother were daily-wage workers when I was growing up. They would go to the agricultural fields every day, and our family depended entirely on what they earned that day. This was the reality of my childhood," he tells The Better India . Some children entered the workforce. Others left school because there was little support at home. His parents nevertheless encouraged him to study. After school, he went to DNR College in Bhimavaram for intermediate and then joined the College of Engineering at Osmania University in Hyderabad, where he studied mechanical engineering from 1986 to 1990. He began his professional career in 1991 and spent the following decades working across India and overseas, including in Nigeria, Kuwait, and the UAE. Today, he works as a lead contracts engineer in Abu Dhabi. But while his career took him away from Yernagudem, what he had seen there stayed with him. "I saw children my age being pulled out of school, not because they lacked ability or ambition, but because their families could not afford to keep them there." Some children entered the workforce. Others left school because there was little support at home or because they had fewer opportunities to learn beyond the classroom. "What struck me most was the inequality of opportunity. The gap was not about intelligence or potential, but about access," he says. It started with a question among childhood friends In 2010, while spending time with childhood friends in Yernagudem, Swami began discussing how they could give something back to the community they had grown up in. Their answer was education. They wanted to 'gift education' to children they would later call V-Kids, beginning in their own village. On 13 January 2011, the Pragathi Association for Rural Development was registered as a society. The organisation later came to be known as PARD INDIA. Swami was already working abroad, and he continued his career while he and his friends began building the initiative around their existing jobs, local volunteers, and people from the communities they wanted to work with. The first programme was launched in August 2011 at the Government MPP Special School in Yernagudem, where Swami had studied. It began with 50 children from Classes 4 and 5. What happens when the school day ends? For many children in these villages, the challenge was finding someone to help them with their studies after school. Their parents often worked as agricultural labourers or in other daily-wage jobs, returning home late with little time to help with lessons. Swami and his friends wanted to address this gap. Their first initiative, the After School Education Programme (ASEP), gave children a place to continue learning with guidance once their regular school day ended. "Most of the children we cover have parents who work on daily wages. In the villages, they go to the fields and may not return until four, five, or even six in the evening," the founder says. ASEP runs from 3.30 pm to 5.30 pm, six days a week, offering children two hours of guided learning. They receive help with mathematics, English, science, moral education, and computer skills. They also make time for reading, sports, drawing, debates, competitions, storytelling, guest lectures, and tree plantation activities. Teachers monitor attendance and speak to parents when children begin missing classes. The programme is also meant to catch warning signs before a child drops out of school altogether. PARD INDIA tracks attendance and works with teachers, parents, and local volunteers when children are regularly absent. Swami says the organisation has found that the reasons are mostly tied to circumstances outside the classroom. "Poverty remains the biggest barrier to education. For families living on daily wages, education can feel like a luxury, and when they have to choose between sending a child to school and meeting immediate financial needs, education is frequently sacrificed," he explains. But money is not the only issue. "The challenge goes beyond finances," he adds. "Rural children are just as intelligent and ambitious as their urban counterparts, but they lack exposure, mentorship, digital access, and supportive learning environments." Bringing computers and new opportunities to villages The initiative gradually added other forms of support to address the different challenges that could interrupt a child's education. The Village Knowledge Centre Programme (VKCP) began in August 2012. At the time, internet access was still limited in many villages. Swami personally contributed Rs 8 lakh and helped establish a centre with 15 computers. Children could learn basic computer skills and use programmes such as Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. The centre operated for nearly eight years. Over time, the computers became outdated. The team now hopes to upgrade and expand the programme with CSR support and has approached several organisations for funding. Alongside computer lessons, the programme also offers career guidance and personality development sessions. For Swami, the idea was simple: children growing up in villages should have the same chance to learn new skills and explore career opportunities as children elsewhere. He wanted them to feel confident about their abilities and know that their circumstances did not have to limit their ambitions. Two years later, in July 2014, PARD INDIA launched the V-Kid Scholarship Programme (VKSP). In 2010, while spending time with childhood friends in Yernagudem, Swami began discussing how they could give something back to the community they had grown up in. The programme supports children who may otherwise struggle to continue their education because of financial circumstances, with particular attention to orphans, children of single parents, and economically disadvantaged families. Students apply according to set criteria, after which the organisation tries to connect eligible children with local donors. Support can extend from Class 1 through graduation. The team also runs the V-Kid Knowledge Boost Programme (VKKB), through which children are selected based on merit-based tests and receive longer-term scholarships. An Rs 800 scholarship and the confidence to continue In 2017, Vamisetti Ganesh from Devarapalli Mandal took part in one such examination. His parents were daily-wage workers, and paying for everything the family needed was not always easy. He secured fifth place in the VKKB examination and received an annual scholarship of Rs 800 for six years, covering his education from Class 6 to Class 10. The scholarship was supported by Mr Nageswara Rao, one of the donors. "Because my parents depend on daily wage work, meeting all our family and educational expenses has not always been possible," he says. The scholarship eased some of that pressure. "It helped with school-related expenses and reduced the financial burden on my family," he says. "It also motivated me to take my education more seriously and aim for better academic results." He is now pursuing his graduation. For Madhuri from Yadavolu village in East Godavari district, the scholarship provided similar continuity. She came from a family dependent on daily wages and received a six-year scholarship through the VKKB programme, covering Class 6 to Class 10. Today, she is pursuing intermediate education in Zangareddigudam and hopes to become an engineer. The difference is not always visible in a single examination result. Sometimes it means that a child keeps going to school the following year. 'I want to support people in need' For Yangala Uma Maheshwari from Gopalapuram, education became particularly difficult after she lost both her parents. She had been associated with PARD INDIA since she was six years old and had received support through the VKKB scholarship programme. When she lost her parents, the organisation continued to stand by her. "The most difficult period of my life began when I lost both my parents. Their absence left a void in my life, and I was suddenly faced with uncertainty, emotional pain, and the question of how I would continue my education without them," she explains. The support she received went beyond the scholarship. "During that difficult time, the team stood by me and provided emotional as well as academic support," she says. "Their continued care gave me the strength to keep moving forward." She is continuing her education and now wants to help other people facing difficult circumstances. "I want to support underprivileged and needy people, just as this organisation supported me when I needed help the most," she says. "I hope to become a source of encouragement and hope for others." From 50 children to over 110 villages What began with 50 children in Yernagudem has since spread across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The non-profit now works in more than 110 villages and has influenced more than 550 communities. Its work has reached places including Cheepurugudem, Dubacherla, Nallajarla, Chinnayagudem, Devarapalle, Tyajampudi, Yadavole, Duddukuru, Goplapuram, Rajahmundry, Kakinada, Vijayawada, Abdullapurmet, Kuntloor in Hyderabad, Jafarguda, Rajivgruha Kalpa, Mathuguda, and rural clusters around Visakhapatnam. As of March 2026, the organisation reports 116,841 direct beneficiaries, including children and elders, and 90,494 V-Kids supported through its programmes. Its work has touched 492,567 lives through education, healthcare, nutrition and community empowerment. Within its education work, ASEP alone has provided 569,419 hours of free education to 3,165 children across 79 villages as of 31 March 2026. The Village Knowledge Centre Programme has delivered 33,999 hours of IT training to 538 children and young people. More than 30 students have received annual scholarships through VKSP. These figures cover different programmes, each addressing a challenge that can affect a child's education. A child should not have to leave school simply because there is nobody at home who can help with a difficult lesson, because the family cannot manage an educational expense, or because the child has never been shown what might be possible beyond the village. Namratha is one of the children still at the beginning of that journey. 'I want to become a district collector' Namratha, a Class 5 student, says her after-school classes helped her understand difficult lessons and gave her individual attention when she was struggling. They wanted to 'gift education' to children they would later call V-Kids, beginning in their own village. "Whenever I doubted myself, the teachers encouraged me and reminded me that I could do better," she says. Her confidence has changed too. "I have become more confident in my studies and in myself . Earlier, I would sometimes hesitate when I faced difficult subjects or challenges, but now I feel more comfortable taking them on," she adds. Today, she wants to become a district collector. "I want to complete my studies and build a successful career," she continues. "I also want to inspire other children to continue their education and never give up on their dreams." For Swami, these ambitions are precisely why the work needs to continue. "The greatest reward of this 15-year journey has been seeing children who were once at risk of dropping out now dream of becoming engineers, doctors, teachers, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and community leaders," he says. Keeping children in school takes a village Supporting these children across villages requires a network of people who can stay connected with them and their families. The initiative's work is supported by a 16-member executive committee, directors and advisers, brand ambassadors, project management teams, an IT team, and volunteer committees at the state, district, mandal (an administrative subdivision), and village levels. The founder puts the wider team at around 52 people, including full-time and part-time members, teachers, volunteers, and others involved in its programmes. There are currently around 20 project management team members and a four-member IT team, while the number of people working on individual projects changes according to their requirements. But a large part of the work rests with people who live in the communities themselves. Village committees help connect children, parents, teachers, and local volunteers. They also help identify children whose attendance is falling and encourage families to keep them in school. "This is the strength of our organisation," the founder says of its volunteer network. "Wherever we run the After School Education Programme, we make sure there is a village committee in place. We do not implement the programme without the committee's involvement." The organisation's model has allowed it to remain connected to villages even while Swami continues to work abroad. He brings his professional experience in planning, contracts, and project management into PARD INDIA, while the organisation keeps him connected to the place where he started. "My corporate career and social service journey complement each other," he says. "While my professional role challenges me to manage complex projects and think strategically, my work with this organisation keeps me grounded in the values of compassion, community service, and human impact." More villages, more scholarships and bigger dreams The initiative now wants to reach 20,000 children across 150 villages by 2030 and provide more than eight million hours of free education. It also plans to introduce STEM-based projects in government schools, expand scholarships from Class 1 through graduation, and develop Village Knowledge Centres with computer- and AI-enabled literacy and skills training. For Swami, the work has always been about more than numbers. ASEP runs from 3.30 pm to 5.30 pm, six days a week, offering children two hours of guided learning. "Education is the most powerful catalyst for social change," he says. He has spent much of his adult life working on large projects overseas, but the reason he continues to return to this work is rooted in what he saw as a child. "I firmly believe that lasting change must begin where we come from. Staying involved with the initiative is not just about leading an organisation. It is about honouring my roots, empowering V-Kids, uplifting families, strengthening communities, and making sure that no child's future is determined by poverty or circumstance," he explains. In Yernagudem, that idea now sits alongside a very different kind of future. Namratha is still in school. Ganesh is pursuing graduation. Madhuri is studying towards her next stage of education. Uma wants to help other children who face the kind of loss she did. Their journeys are different, but each began with the chance to keep studying. And that is what Swami has been trying to protect since that first conversation with his friends in January 2010. He wants every child to have the chance to stay in school long enough to decide what comes next. All pictures courtesy PARD INDIA.

items.descriptionOriginal: A US nuclear microreactor has cleared a key safety hurdle ahead of a planned test campaign targeting 60 effective full-power days of operation and at least 150 continuous hours without operator intervention. California-based nuclear technology developer Radiant announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved the Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) for its Kaleidos microreactor. The approval brings the reactor closer to full-power testing at Idaho National Laboratory (INL), where Radiant plans to evaluate its performance under operating conditions. Unlike preliminary tests that establish whether a reactor can sustain a controlled nuclear chain reaction, the upcoming campaign will examine how Kaleidos performs during extended operation. Radiant says the demonstration will be the industry’s only full-power, extended-duration test of a nuclear microreactor to date. However, the reactor must first pass DOE’s Readiness Review before nuclear operations can begin. Testing beyond criticality The planned testing campaign will take place at the National Reactor Innovation Center’s Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (DOME) facility at INL. The five-phase program will begin with initial criticality, the point at which a reactor achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Testing will then progress through increasingly higher power levels, allowing engineers to evaluate the reactor core, instrumentation, and integrated systems under operating conditions. The campaign targets 60 effective full-power days (EFPD) over several months. This represents the equivalent of 60 days of operation at full power, rather than necessarily 60 consecutive days. Another major objective is to demonstrate at least 150 hours of uninterrupted operation at full power without operator intervention. The test would help establish whether the reactor can maintain sustained operation without requiring constant human adjustments. Radiant’s chief nuclear officer, Rita Baranwal, said the approval covers a broader demonstration than initial criticality alone. “This approval for full power demonstration is a first within the microreactor industry. It moves us forward to test our complete reactor system under sustained operating conditions.” The latest approval follows DOE’s acceptance of Radiant’s preliminary safety analysis in February 2026. Toward commercial deployment Kaleidos is a transportable nuclear microreactor designed to provide electricity for military installations, industrial facilities, and locations requiring reliable power. The reactor has a planned electrical output of 1 megawatt and is designed to be transported by land, sea, or air. Radiant built the unit at its El Segundo, California, facility and shipped it to Idaho National Laboratory in August 2026. The company plans to test a reactor design and custom fuel similar to those intended for commercial customers. This approach is intended to generate operating data directly relevant to future deployments, rather than relying solely on smaller experimental systems. Radiant plans to manufacture Kaleidos units at its R-50 facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. The company is targeting its first commercial deliveries to Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado and Fort Benning in Georgia in 2028. Earlier in October, the US Navy also selected Radiant to deploy Kaleidos at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana. These projects reflect growing military interest in compact nuclear reactors that could provide power independently of conventional electricity grids. Before testing begins, DOE’s Readiness Review must determine whether the reactor, supporting systems, and operating personnel are prepared for nuclear operations. If the review is successful, Radiant can proceed with fueling Kaleidos and beginning its planned test campaign. The reactor has not yet demonstrated the full-power endurance or unattended operation targeted in the program.

items.descriptionOriginal: "How much did everyone else score?" For many teenagers, this question matters almost as much as their own marks. A friend has scored 95, a classmate is already preparing for the next entrance exam, and someone else seems to have everything figured out. Suddenly, their own result doesn't feel good enough. Even before the next exam begins, the pressure to keep up has already set in. What starts as a comparison of marks can soon become something more personal: Am I smart enough? Am I falling behind? Why does everyone seem to be doing better than me? For parents, these moments can be difficult to navigate. Telling a teenager not to compare themselves with others may seem like the obvious response, but what happens when they cannot stop? And how can parents help them build confidence without adding to the pressure? Why comparison feels so intense during the teenage years Dr Gurbani Kohli, a child and adolescent psychologist with over 11 years of clinical experience, has worked with more than 9,000 children. She is the founder and clinical director of HealG A Child Clinic and a senior consultant child psychologist at Apollo Cradle, New Delhi. Her work involves supporting children, adolescents, and families navigating developmental, emotional, behavioural, and learning concerns. In her experience, when teenagers compare themselves with their peers, the issue often extends beyond marks or achievements. Child and adolescent psychologist Dr Gurbani Kohli encourages parents to understand the emotions behind a teenager's comparisons rather than dismissing them. Photograph: (Gurbani Kohli) "When a teenager says, 'Everyone is ahead of me,' they are usually not making an objective assessment of everyone around them. They are expressing how they currently feel about themselves," she says. Adolescence is a period when identity and self-worth are still developing. Peers become increasingly important as teenagers try to understand where they fit in and how others perceive them. A disappointing exam result, a friend's achievement, or being left out of a group can feel particularly significant at this stage, when emotional regulation and perspective are still developing. "Often there is a deeper emotional question underneath the comparison: 'Am I good enough?' 'Do I belong?' or 'Will people value me and my opinion?'" Dr Kohli explains. A teenager who performs poorly in one exam may conclude that they are not good at academics altogether. Someone who misses out on an opportunity may interpret it as proof that they are falling behind. Understanding what lies beneath these conclusions is the first step towards helping teenagers navigate them. When marks become a measure of worth Academic competition can intensify these feelings because exam results are visible, easy to compare, and frequently discussed among families and peers. Questions such as "How much did everyone else get?" can shift a teenager's attention from learning to ranking. Even comments intended to motivate can add to the pressure. "Your sister got such good marks," "Look how well behaved she is" or "You used to do so much better" may leave a child feeling that they are being measured against someone else. When a friend performs better in an exam, a teenager may begin questioning their own abilities and self-worth. Photograph: ( iStock ) Dr Kohli advises parents to notice when comparison begins affecting a teenager's behaviour or confidence. Repeatedly saying they are "not good enough", giving up because they expect to fail, withdrawing from friends or losing interest in activities they once enjoyed are signs worth paying attention to. Some comparison is normal during adolescence. But when it starts shaping how a teenager sees themselves or interferes with everyday life, parents should look beyond the immediate trigger. Listen before offering reassurance When a teenager comes home upset because a friend scored better or secured an opportunity they wanted, a parent's instinct may be to offer perspective. They might say, "Don't be jealous", "You should be happy for your friend," or "There are so many children doing worse than you." Although well-intentioned, these responses can make a teenager feel that their disappointment is unreasonable. "I always believe in connection, not correction," says Dr Kohli. Instead of immediately trying to fix the situation, she suggests acknowledging the feeling and inviting the teenager to talk. Listening without judgement can help teenagers feel understood when they are disappointed by a friend's achievement or their own results. Photograph: ( iStock ) A parent could say, "I can see that this really upset you. Tell me what is bothering you the most." They could also acknowledge the specific disappointment: "Seeing someone else get something you really wanted can hurt." This gives teenagers room to express their feelings without being judged. Parents can then ask what it is about the other person's situation that they wish they had. The answer may reveal a desire for acceptance, anxiety about falling behind or uncertainty about their abilities. Once they understand the concern, parents can help their children work through it rather than dismissing it with general reassurances. Help teenagers recognise their own progress Moving away from comparison does not mean discouraging ambition. It means helping teenagers set goals based on their own needs and growth rather than someone else's achievements. Dr Kohli recommends encouraging children to measure progress against their previous efforts. Instead of asking, "Who scored higher?", parents can ask, "What was difficult for you last time, and what feels easier now?" They can also help teenagers identify skills or habits they want to improve because they matter personally, not simply because a classmate is better at them. For a student struggling with mathematics, for instance, progress might mean understanding a difficult concept or becoming more consistent with practice, even without topping the class. Recognising qualities such as kindness, curiosity and resilience can help teenagers build confidence beyond academic performance. Photograph: ( iStock ) Parents can reinforce this approach by recognising qualities beyond academic performance, including kindness, curiosity, honesty, resilience and the willingness to try again. Giving teenagers opportunities to make decisions, solve problems and contribute at home can also help them build confidence in their abilities. The example parents set matters, too. Teenagers observe how adults evaluate their own careers, appearances, homes and achievements. If comparison is a regular feature of family conversations, children may begin to see it as the natural way to measure success. "Parents don't have to model perfection," Dr Kohli says. A parent who acknowledges comparing themselves with others and explains why they are trying to focus on what matters to them can demonstrate how to recognise and manage the habit. Helping teenagers navigate social media For today's teenagers, comparisons do not end when the school day does. Social media offers a constant stream of other people's achievements, appearances, friendships and lifestyles. Dr Kohli notes that social media does not necessarily create every insecurity, but it can amplify existing ones. Teenagers may end up comparing their everyday experiences with carefully selected glimpses of other people's lives. A complete ban is not always the best solution, she says, because social media is also part of a teenager's social world. Parents can help them identify accounts that leave them feeling inadequate, curate their feeds, and take breaks when they notice these feelings intensifying. If social media is contributing to significant emotional distress, reducing exposure may be appropriate. The aim is to help teenagers become more aware of how online interactions affect them and make healthier choices about their use. Knowing when to seek professional help If comparison becomes persistent and begins affecting daily functioning, parents should consider seeking professional support. Dr Kohli highlights signs such as persistent low mood or anxiety, significant withdrawal, changes in sleep or eating habits, school refusal, loss of interest, hopelessness, self-harm or a strong sense of worthlessness. Social media can intensify feelings of inadequacy, making it important for teenagers to recognise how online content affects their self-esteem. Photograph: ( iStock ) Parents do not need to wait until these difficulties become severe before reaching out for help. Early support can help address distress before unhealthy patterns become deeply established. At home, it also helps to make room for conversations that have nothing to do with performance. Teenagers need to know their parents are interested in their thoughts, relationships and interests, not just their results. Parents can celebrate another child's achievement without turning it into a lesson for their own child. As Dr Kohli puts it, "Someone else's success does not need to become evidence of your child's failure." For a teenager who feels everyone else is moving ahead, the answer is not necessarily another reminder to work harder or think positively. It may begin with listening, understanding what feels difficult and making space for a more personal definition of progress. They do not have to be ahead of everyone else to be doing well. They need the freedom to discover what matters to them and the confidence to keep growing at their own pace.

items.titleOriginal: Gen Z Communicates Differently in the Workplace, but Older Colleagues Can Still Decode Them
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τον Jeff LeBlanc, έναν διαμεσολαβητή μάθησης για διαδικτυακό μεταπτυχιακό στη διοίκηση επιχειρήσεων στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Βοστώνης, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Για όλη τη συζήτηση για τη γεννήτρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Jeff LeBlanc , a learning facilitator for online master of business administration at Boston University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments. Take being late for work. A Gen Z employee in her 20s I spoke with works at a small, locally owned café and restaurant run by an older Gen X owner. When she realized she was going to be late one day, she texted him. He was frustrated. To him, being late was serious enough to warrant a phone call, and a text felt too casual and impersonal. She saw the exact same interaction very differently. “He’s super busy, so I felt a call was going to take up too much time,” she told me. “So I texted. I thought it was more considerate.” Both thought they understood what respectful workplace communication looked like. They just had completely different definitions of it. I study workplace culture and communication, and I see this type of misunderstanding as increasingly common in multigenerational workplaces. And this is becoming more pronounced as Gen Z moves further into the workforce. The oldest members of Gen Z are now approaching 30, while the youngest are in college and high school. What’s distinctive about the older members of Gen Z is that many went through college, internships or their first jobs during the COVID-19 pandemic , when much of our communication moved online and masks often covered half our faces. And there’s a new twist now, as artificial intelligence changes how we communicate all over again. The result isn’t necessarily that Gen Z employees communicate better or worse with their bosses and colleagues than previous generations did. I argue that they have simply learned to do so in a very different environment. When a Text Means Something More The café example is an easy one to dismiss as younger workers preferring texting and feeling that phone calls are for important occasions only. But that misses what I think is the more interesting point: The employee wasn’t trying to avoid her boss. She thought she was respecting his time. For her boss, by contrast, the phone call itself carried meaning. It communicated that she understood the seriousness of being late. Neither one had explained that expectation to the other. Managers shouldn’t assume employees attach the same meaning they do to a particular form of communication. If being late requires a phone call, they need to say so. A two-minute conversation about expectations can prevent both people from walking away from an interaction believing the other was disrespectful. Another common stumble concerns openness, which might feel like oversharing. One Gen Z worker I spoke with had recently started a job at a large New England company in a blue-collar industry. He was struggling with severe anxiety and decided to tell his baby boomer manager. The manager was sympathetic, but also uneasy. “It made me feel uncomfortable, if I’m being honest,” the manager told me. “I didn’t want to downplay his anxiety, but I’m not sure I needed to know.” That distinction matters. His reaction wasn’t that anxiety wasn’t real or that his employee should simply get over it. But he questioned how much of it belonged in their professional relationship. Many older workers learned that professionalism is about setting clear boundaries between personal and professional life. Members of Gen Z are coming of age during a period when conversations about mental health and personal well-being are considerably more public. What feels like honesty to one person can feel like oversharing to their boss. This doesn’t mean that managers have to become therapists, and employees don’t have to disclose everything happening in their lives. But both may need to recognize that their comfort level around disclosure isn’t universal. Aleksandra Sapozhnikova on Unsplash, CC BY What younger workers may see as honesty could be seen as oversharing by older colleagues, who tend to keep more boundaries over personal information. Learning to Read a Room When the Room Disappeared Some workplace communication is never spoken at all. Think about how people traditionally learned to read a room. They watched faces around a conference table. They noticed a change in a manager’s tone. Someone caught them after a meeting and quietly explained what had just happened. Now think about someone who was 18 or 19 in 2020. At exactly the age when many young people would have been developing these skills in college, internships and early jobs, the room disappeared. Classes went online. Internships became remote. When people returned in person, masks sometimes made facial communication more difficult. That doesn’t mean members of Gen Z can’t read facial expressions, but we should be careful about assuming everyone had the same opportunities to learn the unwritten signals of professional life. If feedback matters, I believe managers should say it. A disappointed expression on a Zoom call is a poor substitute for a conversation. I Thought That Was Understood Imagine a manager telling a young employee: “I need this by Friday.” The employee sends it back at 4:30 p.m. that Friday afternoon. The manager is annoyed because they intended to review it that morning, make changes and send it along to someone else. The employee is equally confused. The deadline was Friday, and they met it. This deadline mismatch gets at something I have repeatedly encountered in my research with Gen Z workers. In a survey I conducted of 250 Gen Z professionals across industries, clear structural expectations emerged alongside fairness and empathetic engagement as recurring themes. If an employee wants clarity , it shouldn’t automatically be confused with hand-holding. An employee can want autonomy and still want to know exactly what success looks like. “Friday” and “Friday by 10 a.m. because I need three hours to review this” communicate very different expectations. Artificial intelligence may make this issue even more important. We can now produce polished emails, summarize meetings and generate information faster than ever. But more communication does not guarantee more understanding. I believe that may be the larger lesson for every generation working together. We tend to mistake the workplace norms we learned for common sense. They aren’t. They were taught to us by the workplaces, technologies and moments in history in which we began our careers. Gen Z is learning theirs in a very different world. RELATED: In New Book, Therapist Defines 5 Communication Types — Here’s Why It Helps to Know Yours

Η εξοικονόμηση προήλθε απευθείας από τους στόλους ηλεκτρικών οχημάτων μειώνοντας την ποσότητα πετρελαίου που χρειάζονταν αυτές οι χώρες για να εισάγουν. Αυτοί οι αριθμοί προσγειώνονται…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A new analysis by energy think tank Ember finds that six European countries collectively avoided close to $2.2 billion (approximately €2 billion) in oil import costs between March and August 2026. The savings came directly from EV fleets reducing how much oil those countries needed to import. Those numbers land differently now that oil prices have climbed 33 percent since the Iran conflict began in late February 2026. Brent crude traded near $100 a barrel in late October, up from $67 before hostilities started. Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, a 104-mile (167-kilometer) shipping channel carrying about one-fifth of the world’s daily oil and liquefied natural gas supply, has been the main reason why. Europe’s share of a $20 billion shift Globally, the EV boom displaced an estimated 200 million barrels of crude oil, worth around $20 billion, over those six months. China accounts for the largest share: its fleet of roughly 44 million EVs saved $14 billion in oil costs. EU member states accounted for another $3.1 billion. Within Europe, Germany and France led on raw savings, at around $760 million and $560 million respectively. Denmark’s numbers told a different story. Its EV fleet displaced 6.4 million barrels of oil per year as of August 2026, equal to 13 percent of the country’s entire 2025 oil consumption, the highest share in Europe. The UK displaced around $790 million in crude over the six months; the country imported roughly $27 billion (approximately £21.5 billion) worth of crude in the preceding year. The security dividend Global EV sales grew 11 percent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2026, while combustion engine vehicle sales fell six percent. “The countries that invested in EVs before this crisis are now better protected,” said Euan Graham, a senior energy analyst at Ember, “and a growing number are following.” An EV doesn’t run on oil. At national scale, that translates to real insulation from price shocks driven by conflict or supply disruptions. “Every EV on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets,” Graham said, “and as fleets grow, so does the protection against future supply shocks.” The countries that invested in EVs before oil prices climbed now have a specific dollar figure for what that looked like. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Not every vegetable belongs in a backyard garden. Some take up space, demand attention, and still cost more to grow than to buy once you factor in seeds, soil, and the time it takes. But some crops genuinely save you money, and if your grocery bill has been creeping up, those are the ones to plant. Robert Westerfield , a horticulture specialist at the University of Georgia , and Damon Abdi , assistant professor at the Louisiana State University AgCente r, both weigh in on what pays off at home. Seven vegetables made the list. Herbs Westerfield describes herbs as “so forgiving,” and the economics back that up. Fresh herbs are among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store, and a purchased bunch often goes partly to waste before you get through it. A plant in your garden means you take what you need, when you need it, and nothing wilts in the back of the drawer. Rosemary is an especially smart first choice. It’s evergreen, drought-tolerant, and flowers in a way that looks good in the garden, not just the kitchen. Abdi recommends it specifically because you can harvest on demand rather than buying packaged herbs that “can languish if left unused.” Peppers Peppers are resilient in a way that a lot of vegetables aren’t. Westerfield calls them cold-hardy and says they “come through disease and insects better than anything.” They need consistent water and well-draining soil, but they produce over a long season, and fresh peppers aren’t cheap. Tomatoes Cherry tomatoes are the easiest entry point. Westerfield recommends starting with one or two plants, which he says will supply you through the season with “less trouble than the larger ones.” Give them a trellis or something to climb and they’ll mostly look after themselves. Green beans Green beans can be seeded directly into the ground, no transplants needed, and they produce heavily once they get going. “If you take care of them, you can harvest into the summer,” Westerfield says. They’re a forgiving crop and a reliable one, which makes them a sensible place to start. Asparagus Asparagus is a different kind of investment. Both Westerfield and Abdi recommend it, but the payoff takes patience. The first year or two are about establishment. By the third and fourth year, the harvest grows. A well-maintained bed can produce for up to 20 years. “Asparagus is pricey up front and takes a little time and effort, but it’s perennial once you get it established,” Westerfield says. “You’ll have it basically for life. They can keep on loving you as long as you love them.” Abdi notes that asparagus does best where winters are cool, and that gardeners in warmer climates should look for cold-hardy varieties bred for those conditions. Cucumbers Cucumbers produce heavily and pickle well, so a good summer harvest can stretch well into winter with a few jars on the shelf. Keep them off the ground by growing vertically, and they’ll stay healthier through the season. Squash Squash is easy to grow, though squash bugs and squash vine borers can derail a season quickly if you let them get ahead of you. Stay on top of those two pests, and you’ll come away with a solid harvest. One honest caveat Westerfield is all in on home growing, but he’s clear-eyed about the work involved. It takes time, effort, and real upfront cost. “You know what you put on it and you know where it comes from,” he says. “Usually, the taste and quality are outstanding. There’s nothing quite like fresh tomatoes and sweet corn out of the garden.” The garden only saves money if you’re harvesting and eating what you planted, so starting with the vegetables your household already goes through most is how you make sure it does. items.title: Οι Millennials ανησυχούν όλο και περισσότερο για το ότι οι γονείς τους Boomer είναι κολλημένοι στα τηλέφωνά τους
items.titleOriginal: Millennials are growing concerned about their Boomer parents being glued to their phones
items.description: Οι Millennials δεν απέφευγαν ποτέ να μοιραστούν τα συναισθήματά τους για τους Boomer γονείς τους (και τις ικανότητες των παππούδων τους) στο Διαδίκτυο. Οι Millennials ενώνονται για άλλη μια φορά για να συζητήσουν μια παρόμοια παρατήρηση σχετικά με την απογοητευτική χρήση τηλεφώνου από τους γονείς τους Boomer. Σε ένα νήμα του Ιουλίου 2025 σχετικά με τις διαφορές γενεών στο subreddit r/generationology…
items.descriptionOriginal: Millennials have never shied away from sharing their feelings about their Boomer parents (and their grandparenting abilities ) on the Internet. Millennials are once again uniting to discuss a similar observation about their Boomer parents’ frustrating phone use. In a July 2025 thread about generational differences on the r/generationology subreddit, Millennial member Old-Beautiful-3971 shared their frustrating experience with their Boomer parents who are perpetually on their phones. “My parents are on the very young end of being ‘boomers’. For some reason they’re both acting like me when I was 20… that is to say, gluuuued to their phones,” they wrote. “I tried to have an important conversation with my dad this morning and he did not once look up (and I’m certain he was scrolling through Instagram videos).” An older man using a cellphone. Photo credit: Canva They went on to add, “The only difference is that when I was 20 he could, and would often say ‘Look at me when I’m talking to you. Put that thing away.’ But if I said that to him now he’d get defensive and probably yell at me for being disrespectful. What the heck???” Fellow Millennials agreed The passionate post got a rousing response from fellow Millennials who have experienced the same thing with their Boomer parents. “I have noticed it too and it makes me feel even weirder for having developed in the habit of flipping my phone face-down with my hands folded on top of it to let the person know that I’m listening for that they have my attention,” one commented. “And to think that it’s coming from the generation that tells everybody else that phones and TV will rot your brains.” Another shared, “My parents are visiting me right now. My dad is glued to his phone, even at the table during meals. Never once participating in the conversation except to point at the salt. This is the same man who would have screamed at me for bringing a book to the dinner table.” Others could commiserate about the role-reversal. “I’ve noticed this with my parents. It seems like I’ve switched places with them. I’m trying to use the online world less where as they are using it more and more,” one commented. A man looking pensive with phone in hand. Photo credit: Canva When phones take over family time Some Millennials noted that their Boomer parents’ phone use has impacted other activities they attempt to do together. “It’s become so difficult to watch a movie with my parents. I tell them to put away their phone. Sometimes movies take two days to finish,” another shared. Many Millennials also shared how they communicate with their parents when they notice it. “I am witnessing that as well, my boomer mom and my almost gen z brother visit and they are both glued to their phones. I try and ask if they can put them away because I don’t like my little son to see people like that. I do scroll but never when I am with him,” one Millennial shared. Researchers have a name for this: “phubbing,” or phone snubbing, which a 2016 study linked to lower relationship satisfaction among romantic partners. A related term, “technoference,” describes how parents’ device use interrupts family time, and research on parents has tied it to more behavior problems in children over time. Another added, “I stopped visiting my boomer mom for awhile. I told her to her face that I couldn’t stand the fact that I took the time to drive to her, which I really hate driving, it scares me and I’m not very good at it, and spend MY time with her only for her to be on her phone most of that time. I stopped calling her too because of all the times she’d put me on hold to take another call and then tell me that she’d have to call me back, but she never did. I still rarely call her. I just text so it’s less intrusive and hurtful for me. Now when I visit, her and her husband stay off their phones. They turn the TV down and only put quiet music on instead of blaring whatever crap they were watching. I did thank them for it.” Gen X isn’t off the hook either However, a Gen Z commenter was quick to point out that Gen X is guilty of the same habit. “My gen x parents are hella addicted to their phones (I’m 22 for context),” they wrote. “I’m not saying i’m not, but it’s really hypocritical when they’ll be bitching at me about ‘playing on my phone too much’ when they’re literal ipad kids lol. the reality is, screens and social media are addicting to ANYONE, regardless of age.” Other Millennials pointed out that it’s not just certain generations that are addicted to their phones. “I’m guilty of it as well. Everyone is at risk of screen addiction in this era,” another noted. And another Millennial quipped, “Phones are addictive, that doesn’t just like go away with oldness.” The data suggests they have a point: Pew Research Center’s 2025 survey found that 63% of adults ages 18 to 29 say they use the internet “almost constantly,” compared with 33% of those ages 50 to 64 and 14% of those 65 and older, even though 90% of adults 50 to 64 now own a smartphone. What’s with Boomers and their phones lately? by u/Old-Beautiful-3971 in generationology Phones are tough on every generation If there’s a takeaway from this thread, it’s that the phone gap is smaller than it feels. Millennials remember being told to put the screen away, and now some are watching their parents do the very thing they were scolded for. But as plenty of commenters pointed out, nobody is immune. Whether you’re 22 or 62, a phone is built to hold your attention. Maybe the real fix isn’t pointing fingers across generations, but doing what the commenter with the quiet TV and the put-away phones did: just say something, and see what happens. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Millennials are growing concerned about their Boomer parents being glued to their phones appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια μελέτη παρακολούθησε «χαρισματικά» παιδιά για περισσότερα από 50 χρόνια. Εδώ είναι τι μάθαμε για αυτούς.
items.titleOriginal: A study followed ‘gifted’ kids for over 50 years. Here’s what we’ve learned about them.
items.description: Στη δεκαετία του 1960, ο ψυχολόγος Julian Stanley συνειδητοποίησε ότι αν έπαιρνες τους καλύτερους μαθητές της έβδομης τάξης από όλη τη χώρα και τους έδινες τυπικές εισαγωγικές εξετάσεις, αυτά τα παιδιά θα βαθμολογούσαν, κατά μέσο όρο, περίπου όσο και ο τυπικός τελειόφοιτος του λυκείου. Ωστόσο, οι μαθητές της έβδομης τάξης που σημείωσαν εξίσου καλά ή καλύτερα από τους μαθητές του Λυκείου, ο Στα…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the 1960s, psychologist Julian Stanley realized that if you took the best-testing seventh graders from around the country and gave them standard college entry exams, those kids would score, on average, about as well as the typical college-bound high school senior. However, the seventh graders who scored as well or better than high schoolers, Stanley found, had off-the-charts aptitude in quantitative, logical, and spatial reasoning . In other words, they were gifted . In the 1970s, Stanley and his team launched a full-scale study , identifying many of America’s gifted kids and tracking them throughout their lives. The study, called the Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth (SMPY), never ended and is now more than 50 years in the making. It has followed more than 5,000 kids from middle school into adulthood. The study’s first two groups of participants, about 1,650 people, were identified as being in the top 1% of mathematical reasoning ability. When researchers checked in on them four decades later , 4.1% had earned tenure at a major research university, 2.3% were top executives at name-brand or Fortune 500 companies, and together they had secured 681 patents. Needless to say, a lot has changed with how students are today compared to 50 years ago. Stanley died in 2005, but the study continues at Vanderbilt University, where psychologist David Lubinski helped bring it in 1998. Lubinski, now a professor emeritus, and Camilla P. Benbow, dean of Vanderbilt’s Peabody College, still co-direct it. Why this study matters so much It’s not a stretch to call this one of the biggest and longest-running studies on intellectual “precociousness.” The results of the study thus far are both fascinating and genuinely surprising, a deeply insightful look into the minds and lives of brilliant children. 1. Some of what we used to think about gifted kids turned out to be wrong Ever heard the saying “early ripe, early rot”? It basically means doing “too much” to foster a kid’s special talents and abilities at too young an age could actually cause harm in the long term. That’s not even remotely true, at least not according to Lubinski. A 35-year SMPY study published in 2020 found that skipping grades and other forms of academic acceleration had no negative long-term effects on gifted kids’ psychological well-being at age 50. That saying might be an outdated example, but Lubinski says there are plenty of other misconceptions still alive today, like the idea that gifted kids are so smart that they’ll “find a way” to excel even if those smarts aren’t nurtured and developed. Not so fast. “They’re kids,” he explains. “They need guidance. We all need guidance.” 2. Intelligence is not the same as passion Quick, what’s the “smartest” career you can think of? Doctor? Scientist? While you do have to be pretty brilliant to work in medicine or science, those are far from the only career paths gifted kids choose later in life. “Quantitatively, gifted people vary widely in their passions,” Lubinski says. Many of the students in the study did end up pursuing medicine, but others went into fields like economics or engineering. Others still were more gifted in areas like logical or verbal reasoning, making them excellent lawyers and writers. “There are all kinds of ways to express intellectual talent,” Lubinski explains. When it comes to doing what’s best for a gifted student, it’s just as important for parents and educators to know what the student is passionate about rather than pigeonholing them in traditionally “smart” fields and registering them in a bunch of STEM courses. Students taking a test. Photo credit: Canva 3. Hard work definitely still matters Measuring a student’s aptitude, their natural abilities, is only one part of the equation when it comes to determining how successful they’ll be in life. Aptitude scores can identify a particularly strong natural skill set but tell us very little about how hard that person might work to excel in that field. Effort, Lubinski says, is a critical factor in determining how far someone will go in life. “If you look at exceptional performers in politics, science, music, and literature, they’re working many, many hours,” he says. (And for the record, there are a lot more important things in life than just career achievement, like family, friends, and overall happiness.) The idea that hard work still matters echoes the “10,000-hour rule,” popularized by journalist Malcolm Gladwell in his book Outliers: The Story of Success . Gladwell argued that people like Bill Gates and The Beatles excelled in part because they put in roughly 10,000 hours of practice. The psychologist whose research inspired the idea, Anders Ericsson, has said Gladwell oversimplified it: what matters is deliberate practice, not a magic number of hours. Students around a computer. Photo credit: Canva 4. Regardless of aptitude, every kid deserves to be treated as though they were gifted The study’s focus is specifically on kids within a certain range of intellectual ability, but Lubinski is careful to note that many of its findings can and should be applied to all students. For example, the children in the study who were allowed to take more challenging courses aligned with their skills and interests ultimately achieved more than those who were not afforded the same opportunity. “You have to find out where your child’s development is, how fast they learn, what are their strengths and relative weaknesses and tailor the curriculum accordingly,” Lubinski says. “It’s what you would want for all kids.” What this means for all kids It may sound a bit like a pipe dream, but it’s a great starting point for how we should be thinking about the future of education in America. After all, the SMPY data doesn’t just tell us something about the kids who tested in the top 1%. It tells us something universal: potential rarely announces itself fully formed. It has to be noticed, challenged, and given room to grow, whether that’s a math prodigy who needs to skip ahead a few grades or a kid with a quieter talent that doesn’t show up on any standardized test at all. Fifty years of tracking some of the most capable people in the country boils down to a pretty simple idea. Pay attention to what a kid is actually good at and actually loves, then get out of the way and let them run with it. This article originally appeared nine years ago. It has been updated. The post A study followed ‘gifted’ kids for over 50 years. Here’s what we’ve learned about them. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: The music of Queen has a profound visceral effect on so many people. Few pieces of art can cause complete strangers to put aside their differences and come together in song, but by golly, “ Bohemian Rhapsody ” is one of them. It would be cheesy if it weren’t so absolutely beautiful. This holds true even in countries where English isn’t the first language, it appears. At Harry Styles’ July 2, 2023 concert in Warsaw, Poland, thousands of concertgoers began cheering as those iconic beginning piano notes penetrated the air. It happened before Harry even took the stage It wasn’t long before the entire stadium was singing along to that beloved tune and acing every single lyric. As one person commented on YouTube, “they sing Queen,” even though English isn’t Poland’s first language. (Poland actually ranks among the top 15 countries for English skills in EF’s English Proficiency Index , but the song’s pull clearly goes beyond language.) The passionate impromptu performance serves as a reminder of how special both Queen and the late Freddie Mercury remain today . “ No other band will ever come close to Queen . They were lightning in a bottle and Freddie was a whale in a teardrop. Once people keep singing his words, FM will live on forever,” another YouTube viewer wrote. Indeed, seeing an entire stadium come alive with “Bohemian Rhapsody,” you can’t help but feel Mercury’s soul return to the mortal plane, as if we’ve all been transported back to that historic Live Aid concert in 1985 when he had the entirety of Wembley Stadium wrapped around his finger for 21 glorious minutes. And then it happened again in Paris Just when you think nothing could top that, in July 2025, pianist Julien Cohen and about 30 pro-level musicians and singers came out of nowhere onto the streets of Paris to pull off an epic flash mob performance of the beloved hit, timed to the song’s 50th anniversary: That’s the true timeless beauty of this song. no matter who is singing it, it’s always a semi-spiritual experience that brings people together in a magical way. This article originally appeared three years ago. It has been updated. The post Thousands of concertgoers in Poland spontaneously sing ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’ and it’s flawless appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Her groundbreaking theory on the origin of life was rejected 15 times. Then biology proved her right.
items.description: Σε όλη τη γόνιμη και διακεκριμένη σταδιοδρομία της, η βιολόγος Lynn Margulis έκανε αρκετές πρωτοποριακές συνεισφορές στην επιστήμη που θεωρούμε δεδομένες ως κοινή γνώση σήμερα. Για παράδειγμα, υποστήριξε την «έννοια της Γαίας» του Τζέιμς Ε. Λάβλοκ, η οποία υποστήριξε ότι η Γη αυτορυθμίζεται για να διατηρεί συνθήκες ζωής. Αλλά με διαφορά, το πιο αξιοσημείωτο της…
items.descriptionOriginal: Throughout her prolific and distinguished career, biologist Lynn Margulis made several groundbreaking contributions to science that we take for granted as common knowledge today . For example, she championed James E. Lovelock’s “ Gaia concept ,” which posited that the Earth self-regulates to maintain conditions for life. But by far, her most notable theory was symbiogenesis. While it was first written off as “strange” and “aesthetically pleasing” but “not compelling,” it would ultimately prevail, and completely rewrite how we viewed the origin of life itself . The paper that changed everything In the late 1960s, Margulis wrote a paper titled “ On the Origin of Mitosing Cells ,” that was quite avant-garde. InThroughout her prolific and distinguished career, biologist Lynn Margulis (1938-2011) made several groundbreaking contributions to science that we take for granted as common knowledge today . For example, she helped develop James E. Lovelock’s “Gaia concept,” which posited that Earth’s living and nonliving systems form a self-regulating system that maintains conditions for life. But by far, her most notable theory was symbiogenesis. While it met plenty of skepticism, including a 1972 Science paper that called the symbiotic theory “aesthetically pleasing” but “not compelling,” it would ultimately prevail, and completely rewrite how we viewed the origin of life itself. The paper that changed everything In 1967, Margulis, then publishing under the name Lynn Sagan, wrote a paper titled “ On the Origin of Mitosing Cells ,” that was quite avant-garde. In it, she proposed a theory: that life evolved through organisms merging together to become inseparable. In essence, she argued that cooperation, not just competition, drives some of life’s biggest leaps. This challenged the neo-Darwinian emphasis on competition and gradual mutation that dominated scientific circles, though it didn’t overturn natural selection. Margulis’ paper was rejected by fifteen journals before getting accepted into the Journal of Theoretical Biology . By the late ’70s and early ’80s, research confirmed that mitochondria (found in plant and animal cells) and chloroplasts (found in plants and algae) were at one time independent bacteria. This showed that cooperation between organisms helped build the machinery inside our cells. And now that fact is written in textbooks, with no real story of the adversity it overcame to get there. The idea is still producing discoveries: in 2024, researchers reported the nitroplast , the first known nitrogen-fixing organelle, which appears to have evolved from a bacterium living inside a marine alga. How sexism nearly buried her work While it is customary for most new scientific theories to be met with criticism, especially those that completely shift the current narrative, many have noted that sexism played a key part in Margulis’ initial lack of acceptance. On more than one occasion, she herself had hinted that women were seen as mothers and wives first, and scientists second. Margulis, who was once married to fellow scientist Carl Sagan, told The University of Chicago Magazine in 2004, “I quit my job as a wife twice. It’s not humanly possible to be a good wife, a good mother, and a first-class scientist.” View this post on Instagram Her most controversial beliefs And yet, Margulis also held other controversial ideas that had nothing to do with her gender. Most famously, she did not believe that AIDS was caused by HIV, and instead believed it was caused by a syphilis-causing type of bacteria, despite there already being decades of research proving otherwise. That view was seen as an endorsement of AIDS denialism, which undermined prevention and treatment efforts. Then later in life, Margulis became a vocal proponent of 9/11 conspiracy theories suggesting government involvement in the Twin Towers attacks. And yet, perhaps this is one of those “you gotta take the good with the bad” situations. Margulis’ contrarian streak may have fueled both these unfounded, even harmful stances and the paradigm-shifting ideas that altered our understanding of life itself. View this post on Instagram And if nothing else, her story shows why science needs both open minds willing to challenge the consensus and rigorous evidence to test every claim. It seems life is, after all, about coming together. This article originally appeared in February. items.title: 13 ερευνητές της ευτυχίας συναντήθηκαν και συμφώνησαν σε 5 κλειδιά για να ζήσουν την «καλή ζωή»
items.titleOriginal: 13 happiness researchers met and agreed on 5 keys to living the ‘good life’
items.description: Καμία αναζήτηση στη ζωή δεν είναι μεγαλύτερη από το να ανακαλύψεις τι σε κάνει πραγματικά ευτυχισμένο. Θα ήταν κρίμα να σπαταλήσετε μια ολόκληρη ζωή γαβγίζοντας το λάθος δέντρο μόνο για να συνειδητοποιήσετε στα τελευταία σας χρόνια τι πραγματικά έχει σημασία. Αλλά δυστυχώς, δεν βρίσκουν όλοι την αληθινή ευτυχία. Μια δημοσκόπηση του 2025 της Gallup διαπίστωσε ότι μόνο το 44% των Αμερικανών είναι «πολύ ικανοποιημένοι» με τη ζωή τους, κάτω από 21 μονάδες…
items.descriptionOriginal: No quest in life is greater than finding out what truly makes you happy . It’d be a shame to waste an entire lifetime barking up the wrong tree only to realize in your final years what truly matters. But sadly, not everyone finds true happiness. A 2025 Gallup poll found that only 44% of Americans are “very satisfied” with their lives, down 21 points from 2020 and the lowest score since the poll began in 2001. To help people better understand what makes humans happy , 13 of the world’s leading well-being researchers got together earlier this year on a Zoom call. Their goal: to share what their 600 total years of happiness research and lived experience taught them about finding the good life. They documented their reflections in a research paper published in the Journal of Happiness Studies . A happy woman having coffee. Photo credit: Canva The overwhelming takeaway is that relationships are the biggest key to happiness. “Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” said Lara Aknin , a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University, who coauthored the study with Harvard University’s Säde Stenlund and Kelsey O’Connor from Luxembourg’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies, in a statement. “We know that having just one person you can count on is extremely consequential. Having more relationships and more communities that you feel a part of compounds that sense of well-being,” Aknin continued. The researchers’ discussion yields five key takeaways: 1. Relationships matter more than almost anything else Several researchers on the Zoom call reported consciously spending more time with loved ones after seeing the evidence from their own research. 2. More money doesn’t mean more happiness Yes, a comfortable income and financial security are important foundations—but once your basic needs are met, added income has less impact on happiness. 3. Meaningful work contributes strongly to happiness Happiness comes from doing work and activities that feel worthwhile and aligned with your values. A smiling man with his arms folded. Photo credit: Canva 4. Happiness can grow through intentional habits Several researchers said they applied findings from happiness science to their own lives, such as expressing gratitude, savoring positive experiences, investing in relationships, listening more deeply, volunteering, and being more socially engaged. 5. Happiness is not about feeling good all the time Well-being grows when people shape their lives around their values, strengths, and relationships, and learn to adapt when circumstances change. The researchers also noted that happiness isn’t just about being dealt a good hand in life. It’s about how you handle your circumstances. Leading models find that 10% of people’s happiness comes from life circumstances, such as where you grew up, relationship status, or employment. However, 40% of a person’s happiness comes from “volitional activities,” or how you choose to spend your time. Happy, smiling children. Photo credit: Canva “That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practicing research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” Aknin said. Unfortunately, many in the U.S. are struggling to find true happiness these days. But the good news is that, according to the world’s leading minds on the subject, we can all choose to be happy, regardless of our circumstances, if we follow their research. And when one person chooses the path of happiness, others will follow. “With many large and threatening realities taking place in the world right now, I sometimes worry that the pursuit of happiness can seem trite. But one reason I remain committed to the scientific study of happiness is that happiness in and of itself predicts a number of valuable outcomes, including the motivation to help other people,” Aknin explained. The post 13 happiness researchers met and agreed on 5 keys to living the ‘good life’ appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η επί 40χρονη δασκάλα βιολιού δακρύζει μετά την έκπληξη αποχαιρετιστηρίου των μαθητών της
items.titleOriginal: Violin teacher of 40 years gets teary-eyed after surprise goodbye performance by her students
items.description: Περισσότερο από πιθανό, είχατε τουλάχιστον έναν δάσκαλο που βοήθησε στη διαμόρφωση του ατόμου που είστε σήμερα. Ίσως σας εξέθεσαν σε ιδέες που σας προκάλεσαν να σκεφτείτε με έναν νέο τρόπο. Ίσως είδαν δυνατότητες σε σένα πριν το δεις εσύ στον εαυτό σου. Οι καλύτεροι δάσκαλοι ενσταλάζουν δεξιότητες και τη χαρά της μάθησης που επιτρέπουν στους μαθητές να δημιουργούν και να αναπτύσσονται για τα επόμενα χρόνια. Nam…
items.descriptionOriginal: More than likely, you’ve had at least one teacher who helped shape the person you are today. Perhaps they exposed you to ideas that challenged you to think in a new way. Maybe they saw potential in you before you saw it in yourself. The best teachers instill skills and a joy of learning that enable students to create and grow for years to come. Nam Yun Kim was one of those teachers. She spent nearly 40 years shaping the world of classical music. Many knew Kim as the “Godmother of Korean Violin.” She was a brilliant soloist who performed all over the world. But her favorite home was in the classroom. In 2014, after almost four decades of teaching in South Korea, her students honored her with a retirement concert. Just when she thought she was giving her final bow, something unexpected happened: a bonus performance that would leave her and the audience in joyful tears. A stage filled with love and music Kim was about to leave the stage when about 100 previous and current violin students revealed themselves. They joined the full orchestra for one final, celebratory moment in honor of their mentor. Teens stood shoulder to shoulder with accomplished international professionals. The common link: they all had Kim as their teacher and had benefited from her tough lessons and kind encouragement. When the music swelled, Frank Sinatra’s iconic anthem, “My Way,” filled the concert hall. It was a tribute built from decades of collective passion, patience, and rigorous dedication. Kim’s appreciative and tearful reaction says the rest. Her life’s work was playing all around her. Why ‘My Way’ fit so well Sinatra’s song looks back on a life lived on your own terms. Kim chose to pour herself into generations of violin students in her own, unique way and accumulated decades of devoted students who blossomed from her teachings. Born in Seoul in 1949, Kim studied violin at Juilliard. In 1974, Kim won first prize at the Tibor Varga International Violin Competition. She went on to play at Carnegie Hall, the Kennedy Center, and the Sydney Opera House. Instead of continuing to tour the world as an international star, Kim returned home to South Korea in 1977 and started teaching. She gave masterclasses at Yale and the Beijing Conservatory. Over the decades, she judged top competitions, and her students rose to the top of the violin world. Some of the acclaimed performers who studied under her include Chee-Yun Kim and Yura Lee. For her artistic efforts, Kim received the Nan-Pa Music Award and the Ok-Kwan Medal from the Korean government. Tears of joy for a legendary mentor Most teachers plant seeds they may never see bloom. Kim got to witness hers flourish all at once in one unforgettable moment. The footage of the surprise serenade at her retirement concert still moves people to tears today. She spent nearly 40 years helping others develop their musical talents and got to hear the results of her students’ work during the tribute. Kim passed away in 2023 at the age of 74. items.title: Ένας ασκούμενος της NASA την τρίτη ημέρα βρήκε έναν πλανήτη με 2 ήλιους. 7 χρόνια μετά, εξακολουθεί να συναρπάζει τους επιστήμονες.
items.titleOriginal: A 3rd day NASA intern found a planet with 2 suns. 7 years later, it’s still fascinating scientists.
items.description: Η ιδέα ενός πλανήτη σε τροχιά γύρω από δύο ήλιους ακούγεται σαν επιστημονική φαντασία. Πιο συγκεκριμένα, είναι μια ιδέα από το Star Wars: ο φανταστικός πλανήτης Tatooine έχει δύο ήλιους. Αλλά στην πραγματική ζωή; Οι επιστήμονες πίστευαν από καιρό ότι αυτό ήταν αδύνατο. Ωστόσο, το 2011, ανακαλύφθηκε ο πρώτος «περιφερικός» πλανήτης, όπως λέγεται. Τα επόμενα χρόνια αστρονόμος…
items.descriptionOriginal: The idea of a planet orbiting two suns sounds like science fiction. More specifically, it’s an idea from Star Wars : the fictional planet Tatooine famously has two suns. But in real life? Scientists long thought that was impossible. However, in 2011, the first “circumbinary” planet, as it’s called, was discovered. In the following years, astronomers confirmed more and more. But scientists still didn’t understand much about this rare phenomenon. In 2019, a new planet with two suns was discovered by an unexpected scientist Wolf Cukier was just a high school junior when he began a summer internship at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in 2019. Simply put, he was a data jockey. His job was to dig through extensive data on variations in star brightness captured by NASA’s TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite). On just his third day looking through the data, Cukier noticed something weird. All indications pointed to a stellar eclipse in a distant solar system called TOI 1338. A stellar eclipse is when one star passes in front of another in a binary system, or a system with two stars. “But the timing was wrong,” Cukier said, per NASA. Instead of an eclipse, he realized he was looking at a new planet. High school intern discovers planet TOI 1338 b The planet, clocked by then 17-year-old Cukier on just his third day on the job, became known as TOI 1338 b. Not the catchiest name, of course, which is why some informally call it “Wolftopia” after its discoverer. It lives about 1300 light-years away in the constellation Pictor. TOI 1338 b is a fascinating case. It orbits two stars: one noticeably larger than Earth’s Sun and the other slightly smaller. The stars orbit each other while the planet, about 6.9 times Earth’s size, orbits both. For its part, Wolftopia is extremely large but has an extremely low mass. Its density qualifies it as a “super-puff” exoplanet. Circumbinary planets like TOI 1338 b are difficult to detect. Scientists agree they are relatively common, even though we’ve confirmed only about 18 so far. But their unusual light patterns make them tricky for algorithms to identify. Luckily, the eager and very human eyes of Cukier were on the case. A paper published in The Astronomical Journal featured TOI 1338 b, and Cukier was even listed as a co-author. That makes him one of the youngest co-authors ever on a NASA-related scientific discovery. (He remains ever so slightly edged out by 16-year-old Pritvik Sinhadc , who co-authored Astrobiology Primer 3.0 in 2020.) 7 years later, Cukier and TOI 1338 b have a bright future Cukier’s story was a media hit when it first occurred about seven years ago. But the tale doesn’t end there. TOI 1338 b remains of great interest to scientists. In September 2026, the world’s most powerful telescope—the James Webb Space Telescope —set its sights on the planet to analyze its atmosphere. Though astronomers have discovered over a dozen circumbinary planets, we still don’t know much about them. The light, heat, radiation, and gravitational pull of two suns undoubtedly create weather patterns and surface conditions unlike anything scientists have seen. Once the analysis is finished and released, it can tell us more about how planets form and help us identify even more Tatooine-like circumbinary planets in the future. As for Cukier, he’s still shooting for the stars as an Astronomy and Astrophysics PhD student at the University of Chicago, no doubt motivated by the fact that a discovery on his third day on the job continues to pay dividends in the scientific community.
