items.descriptionOriginal: This Sunday, the clocks will “fall back”—as the battle over daylight saving time continues. In July, the House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. But research shows that daylight saving time doesn’t actually save energy or increase productivity. Instead, sleep researchers like Susan Kohl Malone , assistant professor at New York University Rory Meyers College of Nursing, agree that daylight standard time is more aligned with our biology. The later sunrise of daylight saving time “leads to permanent disruption of our natural biological rhythms. We need morning sunlight to get us up and going,” explains Malone. Malone notes that switching the clock in the spring comes with its own issues, including an increase in car accidents and heart attacks in the week that follows. “Changing clock times is not good for us, but the bill now in the Senate would lock Americans out of sync with the sun,” she writes in the Boston Globe . “A brighter winter evening is a poor trade for a darker, groggier, unhealthier winter morning.” Source: New York University The post Why permanent daylight saving time is a bad idea for health appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: New research explores how perceptions of immunity can shape vaccine decisions and how personalized feedback may help people better understand their protection. When it’s time for another vaccine, many people may ask themselves a familiar question: Do I really need another one? The answer may depend, at least in part, on how protected they think they already are. Allie Sinclair, an assistant professor of psychological sciences and director of Rice University’s Learning & Behavior Change Lab, and her collaborators at Duke University found that people often misjudged their level of immunity to COVID-19. Many believed they were more protected than their vaccination and infection histories suggested, while others underestimated their protection and may have been more concerned about their risk than necessary. Those perceptions matter because what people believe about their immunity can influence whether they get vaccinated, take a diagnostic test when symptoms appear, or take other steps to protect their health. The study in PNAS Nexus sought to better understand why people were not staying up to date on recommended COVID-19 vaccines. The researchers’ earlier work pointed to a potential blind spot: People may know another vaccine is available but believe they are already sufficiently protected. If someone feels overconfident in their protection, they might believe that a vaccine dose doesn’t offer much benefit. “We expected that factors like inconvenience and concern about side effects would be important, but to our surprise, we found that some of the most common reasons were related to overconfidence in immunity,” Sinclair says. “People believed that they were still protected and so didn’t stand to benefit from a vaccine dose.” That led the researchers to develop an interactive “ Immunity Estimator ” tool that gives users personalized feedback about their likely protection against COVID-19. Users enter the approximate month and year of previous COVID-19 vaccinations and infections. The tool then estimates their likely protection against infection and severe disease based on factors including the number and timing of those events, changes in the virus, and the rate at which antibodies decline. Researchers tested the approach with 882 US adults, ages 18 to 93. Participants received either personalized feedback from the Immunity Estimator, an informational flyer produced by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or a modified version of the flyer that included information about waning immunity. The researchers aimed to test whether the personalized feedback about immunity was more effective than these existing, impersonal methods of encouraging vaccination. The personalized approach was the most effective at bringing participants’ perceptions of their risk more closely in line with actual risk (estimated based on each person’s history of vaccines and infections). It worked in both directions, increasing perceived risk among people who underestimated it and decreasing perceived risk among those who overestimated it. The effect was particularly strong among older adults, who are more vulnerable to severe disease and can most benefit from maintaining protection. Sinclair says the Immunity Estimator was designed to tap into two processes involved in how people learn and make decisions. “First, we used corrective feedback because surprising information, or prediction error, engages brain systems that support learning and belief updating,” she says. “Second, we gave participants personalized information because self-relevance is a key part of the brain’s value calculation system, used to guide choices.” Simply put, general information about vaccines or waning immunity may not resonate in the same way as information that shows someone what it could mean for them personally. And the effect lasted. When researchers followed up two months later, participants’ perceptions of risk remained more closely aligned with the researchers’ estimates. Among those who were eligible for an updated vaccine but had not received one when the study began, participants who received information about waning immunity also reported higher vaccine uptake than the national increase during the same period. The researchers caution that the study was not large enough to establish significant differences in vaccine uptake among the three intervention groups. Still, the results suggest that addressing what people believe about their existing immunity could be an important part of vaccine communication. “Prior studies have shown that interventions that focus on just providing information or increasing knowledge tend to have very weak downstream effects on beliefs, intentions and behaviors,” Sinclair says. “Giving people personalized information that targets specific beliefs related to a behavior can be more effective.” Although the research focused on COVID-19, Sinclair sees broader potential for the approach. It could be adapted for recurring vaccines such as the annual flu shot, though researchers would need to develop disease-specific ways of estimating immunity. The implications could extend beyond vaccines. Misjudging personal risk can shape other health decisions, from whether someone takes a diagnostic test when symptoms appear to choices about preventive care and healthy behaviors. “Our beliefs about personal risk and protection are foundational for many preventative health behaviors, like getting an annual checkup or living a healthy lifestyle,” Sinclair says. “Providing personalized feedback could help people make more informed decisions in many areas of life to help them stay healthy.” Source: Rice University The post Perceptions of immunity shape vaccine decisions appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Reading Time: 3 minutes Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist Replacing a car is a big decision. Replacing two familiar journeys can be a smaller, more useful experiment. An e-bike may suit a trip to work, a grocery pickup, or a visit to the library without needing to handle every journey in your week. The starting question is not “How far can this bike go?” It is “Which journeys can I repeat comfortably, legally, and with a workable backup?” This checklist helps turn that question into a practical plan rather than a promise about distance, money, or carbon savings. 1. Define the two trips you want to replace Look at an ordinary week and choose journeys you currently make by car. Start with predictable destinations, manageable loads, and flexible arrival times. An appointment with no margin for delay is probably not the easiest first attempt. Be clear about counting: an outward journey and its return are two one-way trips, but one round-trip outing. Write down which definition you are using. Two bike rides do not necessarily replace two car journeys if someone still drives the same route to collect you or your shopping. 2. Find the calmer route, not just the shortest Compare a cycling map with your knowledge of local streets. Look for lower-traffic connections, suitable crossings, and routes where you feel comfortable managing the bike. A small detour may be worthwhile if it avoids a difficult junction. Inspect the awkward details: where does a bike lane end, how do you cross a busy road, and is the destination entrance accessible? Check current local rules for your bike’s class and the roads or paths you plan to use. An app’s suggested route is not proof that access is legal or conditions are suitable. 3. Budget door-to-door time Allow time to unlock the bike, load bags, negotiate crossings, park, and get ready at your destination. Do not base your schedule on the motor’s assistance cutoff or a brief top-speed reading. Neither tells you the average speed of an entire journey. Try the route without an important deadline. Record the complete travel time and how it felt, then add a buffer appropriate to your schedule. 4. Plan battery use for the whole outing Include the return leg, any errands, and a reasonable detour. Advertised maximum range is not a dependable prediction for your route. Hills, wind, temperature, assistance level, load, battery condition, and other factors can change consumption. Begin with short, familiar rides and note battery use under your own conditions. Leave a conservative reserve rather than planning to arrive empty. If charging at work is part of the plan, confirm permission and a suitable location first. Follow the bike and battery manufacturer’s charging instructions; do not assume any available charger is compatible. 5. Solve parking and carrying before leaving Know where you can lock the bike at both ends. Check whether the parking arrangement works with the frame, your lock, and the property’s rules. If stairs or lifting are involved, assess whether you can manage the bike safely before relying on that access. Pack a realistic load for a practice ride. Secure bags so they cannot interfere with steering, wheels, or braking, and respect the bike’s and rack’s stated limits. Check tire condition and pressure, brakes, lights, and load security before departure. A lighter shopping trip may be a better starting point than a weekly household shop. For a practical example focused on weekend outings, FavoriteBikes’ guide to planning e-bike errands covers stop order, bags, cargo balance, and battery margin. Adapt those planning ideas to the trips you actually want to replace. 6. Decide when not to ride Choose your fallback before you need it. Transit, rescheduling, a lift, or using the car may be appropriate when conditions exceed your ability or the bike’s limits. Check transit rules in advance, including restrictions on e-bikes, batteries, and available carrying space. Rain, darkness, strong winds, snow, and ice can change the decision. Clothing and equipment do not make every route safe, and motor assistance does not remove traction or braking risks. Avoid an unsuitable route rather than treating two weekly trips as a target that must be met regardless of conditions. 7. Keep a simple two-week record For each attempt, note the journey replaced, door-to-door time, battery use, load, conditions, and any difficulty. Include the days you chose not to ride. Those decisions help reveal whether the plan works beyond an unusually easy day. If you compare costs, distinguish avoided fuel or parking from car expenses you still pay, and include relevant bike costs. Do not assign a fixed emissions saving to every ride: the result depends on the vehicle journey actually displaced and the comparison being made. Keep the routes that fit your life, revise the difficult ones, and leave room for other transport. The useful outcome is a repeatable choice—not a perfect score or a commitment to give up the car. The post Can an E-Bike Replace Two Car Trips a Week? A Practical Route-Planning Checklist appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Το νερό της βρύσης του είχε μετατρέψει σαλ…
items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia Hyderabad is facing a serious water crisis. One of its main reservoirs has dropped to just 13%, and 6,000 water tankers are being booked every day. But what if the solution lies in a simple idea that helped Chennai fight its own water crisis? In 1995, Professor Sekhar Raghavan noticed something alarming. His tap water had turned salty because falling groundwater levels allowed seawater to seep in. Chennai received plenty of rainfall, but much of that water was going to waste. Instead of waiting for someone else to act, he began promoting rainwater harvesting. His idea was simple: collect rainwater from rooftops, driveways and other surfaces, filter it, and allow it to recharge underground aquifers. He cycled door to door, convincing residents to adopt the system. Many dismissed his efforts. But he persisted. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting mandatory in buildings. Groundwater levels reportedly rose by nearly 20 feet, helping Chennai improve its water security. For around 15 years, the city benefited from this approach. But there was a problem. Poor maintenance, clogged filters and neglected recharge pits weakened many systems. When Chennai faced another severe drought in 2019, the city once again came dangerously close to running out of drinking water. Today, Chennai is exploring solutions such as sponge parks and underground rainwater capture systems to strengthen its water resilience. The lesson? Rainwater harvesting isn't just about installing systems. It's about maintaining them, protecting groundwater and making every drop count. With Hyderabad facing mounting water stress, could Chennai's experience offer a way forward? Should Hyderabad make rainwater harvesting a bigger priority? items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine a dozen people asked to write down what flats in the same apartment block are worth, and each gives a different figure. That is roughly what an IndiaSpend analysis found among Indian Foreign Service officers. At least a dozen of them had declared sharply different values for flats in the same apartment block in Delhi's Mayur Vihar. Each had filed a return as the rules demanded, yet the differences raised an important question: who was checking whether the values were accurate? "That gap between filing a declaration and proving it honest sits at the centre of how India tries to police the wealth of its public servants. Every public servant covered by the Lokpal law must declare assets and liabilities, but the form is only the first link in a longer chain of checks," explains L. Chakrapani, a Chennai-based RTI activist and former senior advocate at the Madras High Court . Someone has to read these returns, compare them with lawful income and act when the numbers don't add up. Here is how that chain is supposed to work, what the rules actually require today, and where it gets weak. What officials have to declare Under Section 44 of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, every public servant covered by the Act is required to declare their assets and liabilities in the form and manner prescribed by the government. The original law required annual returns by 31 July and directed ministries or departments to publish the statements on their websites by 31 August, as set out in a Department of Personnel and Training order. However, the 2016 amendment replaced Section 44 and removed these specific requirements from the Act. Under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, asset declarations were intended to help bring public servants' wealth under scrutiny. In December 2016, the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) said that returns under the amended Lokpal provision did not need to be filed until fresh rules were notified. In September 2022, it confirmed that those rules had still not been issued. Under the original Lokpal framework, the declaration covered the whole household. It included the assets and liabilities of the officer's spouse and dependent children. Officers of the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service already had a similar duty under the All India Services conduct rules, which ask for a return on first appointment. An India Today investigation reported that the return must list immovable property, shares, debentures, postal time deposits, cash including bank deposits, other movable property, and debts and liabilities. It also noted that the rules cover property held in an officer's own name, a family member's name, or anyone else's name. These service-specific requirements continue to matter even where the separate Lokpal declaration framework has been delayed. For example, IPS officers must file annual immovable property returns by 31 January under the All India Services conduct rules. Filing property returns creates a record against which an officer's wealth can be compared over time. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) That last part is telling. The rulebook also accounts for the possibility of officers holding wealth through other people, which is why the checks after the form matter as much as the form itself. Check one: Did the form even arrive? This is the simplest check, because authorities can identify who has failed to submit a required return. The Central Vigilance Commission has told central government officials that not filing property returns gives "good and sufficient reasons for instituting disciplinary action". It expressed deep concern over prolonged delays and in 2020 set 30 November as the deadline for 100% compliance. Even ministers have been late. Hindustan Times previously reported that 14 cabinet ministers and 21 junior ministers in a 77-strong council had not made their assets public, six weeks after the August deadline for declaring them to the Prime Minister. "There should be a mechanism to scrutinise the declarations. Otherwise there is a weakness that every later check tries to fix, since a filed form proves only that someone filled it in," Chakrapani says. The distinction matters. Treating a missing return as misconduct means officials can't wait for an investigation to begin before answering for the omission. Filing also creates a record to measure against later. "Filing gives authorities a baseline, because every later year can be compared with the one before it. Without that baseline, no one can say that wealth has grown faster than income, which is the question that the criminal law eventually asks," he explains. Check two: Are the numbers true? A form can be complete and still be wrong, which is why the differences reported in the Mayur Vihar declarations deserve scrutiny. IndiaSpend asked whether the real worry was that officers misstated values or "just don't care". For ordinary citizens, even seeing these forms has been a struggle. India Today reported that it took "two years of argument and persuasion" with the Department of Personnel and Training and the Central Information Commission, through the RTI route, to obtain just the immovable assets of around 120 secretary-rank officers. That was before the Lokpal Act originally introduced a requirement for ministries to publish annual statements. Although the 2016 amendment removed that requirement from Section 44, property returns filed under certain service rules are still published by the relevant departments. The Prevention of Corruption Act provides for action against public servants who cannot satisfactorily account for disproportionate assets. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) It shows why public access has always been part of the story. "Realistic verification rests on comparing declarations with independent records, mainly income-tax data, since the CBDT already cross-checks elected representatives' affidavits and reports any discrepancies. This rests on the CBDT and Election Commission framework, covered by the Lawyer E-News report, and on the CBDT's 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court," Chakrapani tells The Better India. For elected representatives, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and the Election Commission of India (ECI) have a joint framework for verifying election affidavits. It allows asset disclosures to be checked against tax information and discrepancies to be investigated, according to a Supreme Court order reported by Lawyer E-News. In a September 2017 affidavit to the Supreme Court, the CBDT said it had begun investigating seven Lok Sabha members and 98 assembly members after finding discrepancies in their declarations. The Court had pulled up the government over members whose wealth showed "a massive jump". The department said details would go to the court in a sealed cover, since income-tax investigations are exempt under the transparency law. These checks concern election affidavits filed by candidates. They are distinct from the property returns filed by civil servants, although both raise the same question about independent verification. Check three: What if an official's wealth grows faster than their income? Once a discrepancy surfaces, the Prevention of Corruption Act gives investigators a legal test. The offence has a long history. Section 5(1)(e) of the 1947 Act criminalised property disproportionate to known income, and Section 13(1)(e) of the 1988 Act carried the idea forward before the 2018 amendment recodified it. Section 13(1)(b), as substituted by an amendment that took effect on 26 July 2018, makes it an offence to enrich oneself illicitly during the period of office. The law presumes illicit enrichment when a public servant, or anyone on their behalf, holds money or property disproportionate to known sources of income that they cannot satisfactorily account for. "The Act defines known sources of income as income from lawful sources, which means gifts, loans and savings count only if they can be shown to be lawful. A conviction carries imprisonment of not less than one year and up to seven years, and a fine," Chakrapani says. Tax records and independent financial checks can help investigators identify discrepancies between declared assets and lawful income. Photograph: ( The Hans ) The current Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, however, provides for imprisonment of four to ten years, along with a fine. The punishment was increased from the earlier one-to-seven-year range through an amendment effective from 16 January 2014. The Lokpal can act too. According to Nyaaya, its inquiry wing conducts an initial inquiry into corruption charges against a public servant, and the Lokpal can then file a case before a Special Court. PRS Legislative Research notes that the Lokpal holds power of superintendence over the CBI for cases it refers. This is where the declaration becomes evidence. It records what an officer owned on a given date and who else held property for the family. "A case can then succeed when investigators rebuild lawful income, loans, gifts and savings across the check period, and fail when that accounting has gaps," he says, drawing on his own litigation experience. Check four: Will the evidence hold up in court? Courts examine disproportionate assets cases in two stages. According to a legal analysis published by Casemine, the prosecution must first establish the disproportion. Only then does the burden shift to the accused to account satisfactorily for the assets. A High Court ruling reported by Taxguru shows how this plays out. The court set aside the conviction of two public servants in Chennai because the prosecution had not properly accounted for their legitimate income, loans, gifts and savings. It held that the defence had shown the properties came from lawful sources. Photograph: (AI-Generated) A strong case, then, needs more than a list of properties. Investigators must rebuild a full income and expenditure picture across the entire check period. According to Chakrapani, this is also why accurate declarations matter, since a truthful record of loans and gifts made years earlier can support or undercut a later explanation. Who is monitoring the growing wealth? The system has one gap that courts have already noticed. On 16 February 2018, a Supreme Court bench of Justices J Chelameswar and S Abdul Nazeer directed the creation of a permanent mechanism to monitor the assets of legislators that grow disproportionately to their known income. The bench said such assets "should alarm citizens and voters of any democratic society", according to LiveLaw. The Wire reports that the same bench refused a one-time investigation of named legislators, calling that "selective witch-hunting". It asked for monitoring of legislators whose assets rose by more than 100% by the next election, with findings reaching the appropriate legislature. Lok Prahari later filed a contempt petition, arguing that the government had not complied with several directions. The Wire reported on 24 April 2026 that the Supreme Court had disposed of the petition on 16 April 2026, after finding no wilful disobedience. The permanent mechanism had still not been created eight years after the original judgment. During the proceedings, the Union government pointed to an existing framework between the ECI and the CBDT for verifying asset disclosures. The Court accepted that contempt had not been established, bringing the proceedings to a close. In practice, that leaves verification to existing agencies, which act on complaints, tax discrepancies and criminal investigations. What this means for you The four checks show the different stages at which an asset declaration can be examined, although they do not necessarily follow one fixed sequence in every case. The first confirms that officials file, the second tests whether the numbers hold up, the third compares them with lawful income, and the fourth tests the evidence before a judge. A weak link anywhere can leave a questionable declaration unexamined. For citizens, the practical test is whether these stages are visible. Published returns, publicly reported verification findings and open court proceedings are among the ways outsiders can observe how the system is working. The Lokpal Act originally set the 31 July deadline, while other service rules continue to require property declarations. The Prevention of Corruption Act provides criminal penalties for illicit enrichment. The space between them depends on who is willing to read the forms. A declaration builds accountability only when someone checks it against income and acts on what they find. Eight years after the Supreme Court called for permanent monitoring of legislators' wealth, that mechanism remains absent. The question now is whether the existing checks can provide the scrutiny that the Court had sought. Sources ' Has Supreme Court Agreed to Bury its Own 2018 Mandate on Legislators' Assets?' : by for The Wire, Published on 24 April, 2026 ' The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 – Submission of declaration of assets and liabilities by the public servants ': by Department of Personnel and Training for gconnect.in (office memorandum) ' Section 13 in The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 ': by Government of India (as substituted by Act No. 16 of 2018) for Indian Kanoon, Published on 26 July, 2018 ' No Contempt Made Out Against Union For Not Creating Dedicated Cell To Monitor Legislators' Asset Growth: Supreme Court ': by [byline to confirm] for Lawyer E-News ' 7 MPs, 98 MLAs under I-T lens over assets declaration ': By Hindustan Times, Published on 12 September, 2017

items.descriptionOriginal: A 100th birthday usually calls for cake and candles, yet P Balasubramanian Menon, a lawyer from northern Kerala's Palakkad district, received something rarer and rather more formal. On 9 October 2026, six days before he turned 100 on 15 October, the Kerala High Court approved his designation as a Senior Advocate, timing the decision to coincide with the milestone itself. Chief Justice Soumen Sen began the initiative, and Bar and Bench reported that this might be the first time the court has conferred the rank on a lawyer who practises before the mofussil courts, which sit below the High Court. Bar and Bench calls Menon a trial lawyer, a practitioner who argues disputes before the courts that hear them first. Under Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961, India has two classes of advocates, senior advocates and other advocates. A High Court may formally designate an advocate as senior, with the advocate's consent, if it considers that ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge or experience in law makes him deserving of the distinction. By approving the designation, the Kerala High Court formed that opinion about Menon after more than 76 years in practice. From Madras to Palakkad To understand the honour, it helps to look at where his career began and how it changed direction. Menon comes from a traditional family in Palakkad and studied law at Madras Law College before he began his career in 1950 at the Madras High Court , where he trained under Advocate General Kuttikrishnan Menon. After two years, he returned to Palakkad and worked under the criminal lawyer KS Ramakrishna Iyer. Bar and Bench's 2023 interview records that, like many lawyers of his generation, he had not made law his first choice. The Kerala High Court designated Menon a Senior Advocate on 9 October 2026, days before his 100th birthday. Photograph: ( Bar and Bench ) His early cases were criminal, but an encounter with a judge during a case in Kochi encouraged him to specialise in civil law, which has been his focus since 1952 and remains his main area of practice. LiveLaw reported in 2023 that he continued to practise on the civil side in his hometown. How 73 years of practising law earned him a world record His office, as Bar and Bench described it in 2023, has an old-world charm and countless mementoes, the latest being the Guinness World Record, while a second certificate in a glass frame marks the Indian Book of Records recognition that came a few months earlier. Guinness World Records verified his career in Kerala at 73 years and 60 days on 11 September 2023, making him the holder of the title for the longest career as a lawyer (male). Asked by Bar and Bench whether he had ever imagined such recognition, he said not even in his dreams. Menon surpassed the record set by Louis Triay, a Gibraltar lawyer whose record stood at 70 years and 311 days, according to LiveLaw. Triay died in February 2023 at the age of 94, months before Guinness World Records verified Menon's career. From beginning his career at the Madras High Court in 1950 to practising in Palakkad, Menon has spent decades arguing civil cases. Photograph: ( Facebook/Suma Kanakala ) PTI reported in November 2023 that, with the enthusiasm of a much younger lawyer, he went to his office and the courts every day without fail, met clients and kept his arguments and cross-examinations brief, even at 97. He describes his duty to clients in terms of trust, telling a television channel, "When a party approaches me with a case, he is coming by trusting me." At 100, he still has no plans to retire Three numbers recur in Menon's story, and each measures something different: his age of 100, his more than 76 years of practice according to Bar and Bench, and the 73 years and 60 days that Guinness verified on 11 September, 2023. The gap between the two shows his career continued well after Guinness took its measurement. In the 2023 interview, when he was in his 98th year, Menon said, "I am running 98. I am not even thinking of retirement." He added that he still works to earn his livelihood, and PTI noted that he smiles gently when anyone asks about retirement. The Senior Advocate rank now joins the Indian Book of Records certificate and the Guinness title among the formal recognitions of a career that began in 1950. Menon has said that he hopes the record can inspire others, and his story offers them a gentle lesson: a lawyer who keeps his arguments brief, answers to his clients' trust and smiles when asked about retirement has built the longest career Guinness has verified for a male lawyer, one patient year after another. Sources ' Kerala High Court confers Senior Advocate designation on 100-year-old P Balasubramanian Menon with longest law practice ': by Praisy Thomas for Bar and Bench, Published on 10 October, 2026 'I am not even thinking of retirement: Longest serving lawyer and Guinness World Record holder P Balasubramanian Menon ': by Sara Susan Jiji for Bar and Bench, Published on 16 November, 2023 ' At 97, Kerala man sets world record as longest serving lawyer ': by PTI for The Tribune, Published on 8 November, 2023 ' 97 Year Old Keralite Sets Guinness World Record As Lawyer With Longest Career ': by Navya Benny for LiveLaw ' Designation of Senior Advocates (Unstarred Question No. 489) ': by the Ministry of Law and Justice (answer by D V Sadananda Gowda) for Lok Sabha, Published on 26 February, 2015

items.descriptionOriginal: Before the tigers take over the streets of Thrissur, they have to be painted. For hours, artists cover performers' bodies in yellow, black and red stripes. Masks go on, drums begin to beat, and on the fourth day of Onam, the 'tigers' dance through the Kerala city, prowling and pouncing before cheering crowds. These tigers are people, of course. But the animal they imitate has held a special place in local celebrations for generations. The tradition is called Pulikali, meaning 'play of the tigers'. And hundreds of kilometres away, along Karnataka's coast, another tiger dance carries stories of fear, admiration and protection. Together, these traditions offer a fascinating glimpse into how communities have understood and lived alongside the wildlife around them. How did tigers become part of Onam? Thrissur's Pulikali is believed to be around 200 years old. Its beginnings are often traced to Sakthan Thampuran, who ruled Cochin from 1790 to 1805. Historical accounts offer different explanations of how the dance developed, reflecting the many cultural influences that shaped Thrissur's public celebrations. Today, on Naalaam Onam, trained troupes gather with their bodies painted as tigers and leopards. They dance to the beats of traditional drums such as the chenda, thakil and udukku , sometimes acting out hunters pursuing tigers. Preparing for the performance takes hours of painting and practice. For the crowds that gather in Thrissur, the result is a celebration that brings the tiger into the heart of the city, year after year. Artists spend hours having their bodies painted in elaborate tiger or leopard patterns before dancing to percussion instruments such as the chenda, thakil and udukku. Photograph: (Manojk) Why do people in coastal Karnataka dance as tigers? Along Karnataka's coast, particularly in the Tulunadu region, a similar tradition called Pilivesha, also known as Hulivesha, brings painted tigers into the streets during annual celebrations. Performers paint their bodies in striking tiger patterns and dance through public spaces, keeping alive a tradition that has been passed down through generations. But what makes the tiger such an important part of these celebrations? The answer lies partly in the stories people have told about the animal for generations. In local folklore, the tiger has long represented strength, courage and protection. It has also been an animal people feared, particularly in places where communities lived close to forests. This relationship caught the attention of researcher Rohan Sharma. In a 2024 report for the Wildlife Conservation Society–India, Sharma spoke to performers, organisers and experts to understand Pilivesha's place in local life. His research explored how the tiger became a powerful cultural symbol and how stories about the animal have influenced the way communities understand wildlife. The dance offers a window into the beliefs, memories and traditions through which people have connected with wild animals for generations. Pilivesha documents a cultural relationship through which the animal occupies a place in community life beyond its biological presence in the landscape. Photograph: (Karthy shty) Can these dances change how we see wildlife? Admiring a tiger during a festival is different from encountering one near a village, where people may fear for their safety or livestock. There is no evidence that performing Pulikali or Pilivesha directly prevents conflict with wild animals. But these traditions remind us that people's relationships with wildlife have histories of their own. Sharma's research suggests that conservation efforts can benefit from understanding local beliefs and listening to communities, alongside protecting habitats and addressing real safety concerns. After all, people who have grown up hearing stories about tigers may understand the animal differently from someone who has encountered it only through books or documentaries. When the drums stop and the paint comes off, the festival ends. Yet the stories remain, passed from one generation to another. And perhaps that is where these tiger dances offer their most meaningful lesson. By understanding why communities have long feared, respected and celebrated the tiger, we can begin more thoughtful conversations about sharing our world with wildlife. Sources: 'Celebrating Nature-Culture Relationships: Documenting Cultures and Traditions of Tiger Folklore in Coastal Karnataka through the Annual Pilivesha Celebrations' : By Rohan Sharma, Published in 2024 'Sharing Spaces and Entanglements With Big Cats: The Warli and Their Waghoba in Maharashtra, India' : By Ramya Nair, Dhee, Omkar Patil, Nikit Surve, Anish Andheria, John D. C. Linnell, Vidya Athreya, Published on 23 June 2021 'Pulikali' : By Kerala Tourism

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World Reading Time: 4 minutes If human beings rise, must other life necessarily fall? We rarely ask because we’ve never learned to see beyond ourselves, understanding that cost starts with understanding how we imagined our place in the world. Human beings have become a species capable of deciding the fate of almost everything around us: deciding where forests remain, where roads are built, where rivers flow, where wildlife may move, which animals are confined, and which habitats are altered for human purposes. Yet the power to decide does not necessarily create a right to decide. Beneath these choices lies an anthropocentric hierarchy where human interests are treated as primary while the interests of other living beings are considered secondary whenever they conflict with human preferences. Against this hierarchy, I rely on Martha C. Nussbaum’s capabilities approach to examine whether human interests should automatically prevail when their pursuit restricts the fundamental capabilities of animals. In Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility , Martha places animals in the sphere of justice and argues that justice requires more than preventing suffering. It requires securing the conditions necessary for animals to flourish according to their species-specific nature. The precise content of flourishing necessarily differs between each species. A bird requires opportunity to fly, a fish requires an aquatic environment in which it can swim and behave according to its nature, and a wild animal requires habitat, movement, ecological relationships, and the ability to exist without constant human control. For Martha, the problem is not simply suffering. It is capability deprivation. The human domination over animals is not accidental; it is structural and deeply embodied in our political, cultural, social, and economic systems. It does not arise merely from individual cruelty but from institutional arrangements designed around human benefits. Around the world, animal laws and conservation policies are structured within an anthropocentric framework. Animals are protected, conserved, and regulated not as right-bearing beings, but as resources to be managed for human benefits. Like, in Pakistan, animals are largely protected through welfare-based laws, not through a capabilities-based framework. The primary legislation, such as the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1890 largely focuses on preventing visible cruelty rather than ensuring the flourishing of animals. Similarly, the provincial laws prioritize conservation of wildlife for human benefit rather than justice for animals themselves. The absence of a capabilities-based legal framework means that animals are still treated as objects of ownership and trade. Fish and birds sold on Pakistani streets are not perceived as beings whose rights are violated; instead, they are seen as commodities. They are viewed as property rather than beings of justice, where exploitation becomes habitual, invisible, and unquestioned. Human interests are not morally uniform. Human beings require food, shelter, health, security, transportation, livelihood, and infrastructure. But human societies also pursue convenience, entertainment, aesthetic preferences, commercial profits, and cultural habits. These interests cannot carry the same moral weight. A preference for cheap entertainment cannot automatically be placed on the same level as an animal’s basic freedom of movement. Fish trapped inside transparent plastic bags, under the complete control of a fish vendor on the streets of Lahore. Their aquatic life is reduced to a small plastic world where they remain alive, but are deprived of the space and freedom to live according to their nature. Photo by the author. Commercial tourism cannot automatically justify disturbing wildlife. Infrastructure development cannot justify destroying habitat where an alternative route or design is available. Martha’s framework, combined with necessity and proportionality principle, distinguishes the moral weight of different human claims. First, the human interest must be legitimate and sufficiently important. Secondly, the particular interference with animal capabilities must actually be necessary to achieve that interest. Lastly, where a less harmful and reasonable alternative exists, the more harmful practice should not be permitted merely because it is cheaper, easier, or customary. These tests distinguish human interests into non-essential, significant but non-vital, and vital human interests. Martha makes it clear that unnecessary human interests carry no moral or legal exception when they exploit an animal’s capabilities. Zoo confinement is a clear example of how entertainment and profit function as human interests that undermine animal rights. These animals are removed from their natural habitats and placed in artificial, restrictive environments, often in noisy and polluted urban settings. Zoos deny their freedom of movement, bodily integrity, and natural behavior’s, reducing them to spectacles for human amusement and revenue generation. The same analysis applies to the roadside sale of birds and fish. Birds confined in cages and fish sold in plastic bags are alive but incapable of flourishing. Even when sellers claim livelihood necessity, this interest remains non-essential because alternative businesses are available. The human right to business or livelihood cannot justify the exploitation of sentient beings. When business models depend on violating animal capabilities, they are illegal and should be prohibited. Justice requires banning such practices and supporting alternative livelihoods that do not rely on animal suffering. The commercial activities in protected wildlife areas reflect another form of human interest. Glamping and overcrowding disrupt wildlife migration patterns, feeding habits, breeding cycles, and freedom. While it generates profits, these benefits are not necessary for human survival and cannot justify the erosion of animal capabilities. Deforestation and unchecked urbanization also conflict with animals flourishing. They are built upon a hierarchy that privileges human expansion over interspecies justice. When forests and green belts are cleared for commercial use, animals lose the ecological foundation necessary for their existence. Habitat destruction fragments ecosystems, eliminates nesting and breeding grounds, and increases starvation and human-wildlife conflict. When forests are valued only for timber, and land and rivers are valued for commercial use, animals are reduced to externalities. In these cases, the principle is clear: human interest must be necessary and regulated. Economic gain, entertainment, and convenience cannot justify the deprivation of animal capabilities, particularly when alternatives exist or when such practices serve no essential human needs. If animal exploitation becomes normal and the state fails to regulate unnecessary human interests, the animal’s existence will become impossible. The limitation on human interests does not mean eliminating human freedom, but it means regulating and restricting activities that commodify living beings unnecessarily. Martha’s theory reminds us that animals are not objects of convenience; they are subjects whose capabilities impose limits on our ambition. The fish trapped in plastic, birds in cages, and zoo animals remind us that flourishing is a right, not a privilege, and human interest, no matter how convenient or profitable, must stop where the capabilities of other sentient beings begin. Limiting unnecessary and exploitative human interests is not a moral preference but a legal obligation in a just society committed to interspecies dignity and coexistence. It underscores that human freedom, while important, is not absolute and must yield when it conflicts with the flourishing of other species. The post When Humans Rise, Must Another Life Fall? Rethinking Human Interests and Animal Flourishing in an Anthropocentric World appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials Reading Time: 3 minutes Sustainable polymers and natural rubber are moving to the center of materials science, as new research shows how to design them to reduce their environmental footprint. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber took center stage at a joint symposium between researchers in France and Thailand. The University of Haute-Alsace and Kasetsart University co-hosted the online event across May 2026. The program covered a wide range of materials topics, from energy materials to nanotechnology. One theme stood out clearly across the sessions. Scientists are now designing polymers not just for performance, but for durability, repairability, and better end-of-life outcomes. Dr. Wirasak Smitthipong of Kasetsart University presented one of the symposium’s central ideas. His team studies smart polymers that respond to light and can heal themselves when damaged. These self-healing materials include rubber and hydrogel systems. Special molecular bonds allow damaged sections to reconnect and recover their function, much like scar tissue mending itself. That self-repair ability matters beyond the lab. If a material can signal damage and fix itself, it may not need replacing as often. This applies especially to coatings, adhesives, and composite products, where small damage often forces the replacement of a much larger item. Light also played a starring role in another presentation. Dr. Jacques Lalevée from the Institut de Science des Matériaux de Mulhouse, part of the University of Haute-Alsace, discussed new light-activated processing methods for high-performance materials. His work uses light to trigger chemical reactions in coatings, inks, adhesives, and 3D-printed parts. This approach offers precise control, produces little or no volatile organic compound release, and reacts faster than older methods. That same light-based technique can work with bio-based resins made from natural oils. This points toward manufacturing that uses less energy and allows for localized repairs rather than full replacement. Other researchers tackled the opposite end of a material’s life. Dr. Amornrat Lertworasirikul of Kasetsart University studies how to make polylactic acid, a common bio-based plastic known as PLA, break down more easily after use. PLA already appears in packaging, farming tools, and medical devices. Her team found that adding a small amount, just 3% by weight, of a plant-derived compound helped the plastic become more flexible and degrade faster in water. This research raises an important question for sustainable polymers and natural rubber alike. Should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or simply become easier to repair and reuse? The answer depends entirely on the product. Packaging that gets used once benefits from fast degradation, while structural materials benefit more from durability and repair options. Natural rubber also showed plenty of untapped potential. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber face the same fundamental design question: should a material last for decades, break down quickly, or be easier to repair and reuse? The new research shows that a 3% plant-derived additive can make plastic more flexible and water-degradable, suggesting the answer depends entirely on what the material is made to do. Photo by Lucas van Oort on Unsplash. Dr. Sutee Boonchui presented transparent, flexible films made by blending natural rubber with quantum dots, tiny particles that glow under light. These fluorescent films could improve road safety equipment, making traffic signs and markers more visible. The natural rubber base keeps the material flexible enough for real-world outdoor use. Medical safety also got a rubber-based upgrade. Dr. Kiadtisak Saenboonruang described multilayer gloves made from sustainable polymers and natural rubber, designed to block X-ray radiation more effectively. By layering in a nanoscale bismuth oxide additive, the gloves blocked more radiation than standard single-layer versions. The outer layers of pure natural rubber kept the gloves flexible and comfortable to wear. Tire manufacturing also came under the sustainability lens. Dr. Hassarutai Yangthong showed how fly ash, a waste byproduct from burning coal, can replace some of the zinc oxide typically used in tire rubber production. Zinc oxide use raises environmental concerns when it washes into waterways. Lifecycle analysis found that substituting fly ash lowered several measures of environmental harm, including toxicity to freshwater and marine life. Taken together, these projects reveal a shared philosophy. True sustainability depends on a material’s entire lifecycle, not simply whether it originates from renewable sources. A bio-based plastic that requires enormous energy to produce offers little advantage over conventional options. Likewise, a material that degrades too quickly may not suit long-term applications like construction or safety equipment. Sustainable polymers and natural rubber research is now moving toward this more complete picture. Scientists are learning to weigh performance, repairability, and lifespan together rather than treating them as separate goals. The symposium’s researchers plan to keep exploring how far these smart materials can go. As industries search for greener alternatives to conventional plastics and rubber, this kind of integrated thinking may prove essential to getting the balance right. The post Sustainable Polymers and Natural Rubber Chart a Path Toward Greener Materials appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age Reading Time: 3 minutes From picture books for toddlers to a 400-page field guide, new bat conservation books invite readers of every age into the surprisingly wondrous world of the only flying mammal. Bat conservation books rarely dominate bestseller lists, but a fresh crop of titles released this year proves the subject deserves far more shelf space than it typically gets. Bat Conservation International recently rounded up a dozen standout titles spanning children’s picture books to dense scientific references, each aiming to replace fear of bats with fascination. For younger readers, several bat conservation books lean into storytelling and gentle life lessons. Stellaluna, considered among the first children’s books centered on bats, follows a baby fruit bat raised temporarily among birds after falling from her mother’s roost, ultimately learning that differences need not prevent friendship. I’m Not Scary follows a lonely bat who simply wants companionship despite living somewhere admittedly spooky, offering warm illustrations built around a familiar theme: kindness overcoming fear. Other bat conservation books for children tackle real conservation challenges directly. Bat Count: A Citizen Science Story introduces young readers to white-nose syndrome, the disease that has devastated North American bat populations, following a girl preparing for a community bat count who learns both the crisis facing bats and how ordinary people can help through citizen science. Amara and the Bats follows a similar arc, as a young bat enthusiast discovers her new neighborhood’s bat roosts have vanished due to tree removal, then finds inspiration in other young people already working to protect local bat populations. Additional titles for younger audiences round out the reading list. Little Red Bat explores the dilemma facing bat species that must choose between migration and hibernation as autumn arrives, weaving in facts about tree-roosting habits and camouflage along the way. The Bat Book, narrated from the perspective of a juvenile bat living under a bridge in Austin, Texas, directly addresses common misconceptions children repeat about bats being weird or scary. For adult readers and dedicated naturalists, bat conservation books shift toward deeper scientific territory. The Secret Lives of Bats follows renowned bat photographer and biologist Merlin Tuttle’s decades-long career, beginning with a teenage cave discovery outside Knoxville, Tennessee, that launched a lifetime devoted to bat ecology and conservation across encounters ranging from Kentucky moonshiners to charging elephants. The Weird and Wonderful World of Bats takes a curiosity-driven approach, devoting individual chapters to each bat sense, including echolocation, alongside candid explorations of bat mating behavior and social communication. For naturalists and dedicated readers, recent bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family and Bat Island document the diversity of nearly 1,500 known bat species through detailed photography, distribution maps, and firsthand field research. Photo courtesy of Bat Conservation International . The Genius Bat follows an ecologist’s research travels from Israeli deserts to tropical rainforests, examining how scientists design experiments to study bats’ extraordinary sensory and behavioral adaptations. For readers wanting comprehensive identification resources, bat conservation books like Bats of the World: A Guide to Every Family organize the roughly 1,500 known bat species by suborder, pairing close-up photography with distribution maps and details on diet, anatomy, and physiology. Bat Island narrows its focus dramatically, documenting the 76 bat species found on a single small island in Panama’s Lake Gatun through cinematic photography and firsthand research from Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute scientists. Rounding out the collection, Bats: An Illustrated Guide to All Species offers a 400-page reference dividing global bat diversity along modern phylogenetic lines, paired with extensive photography documenting species across every studied region. Together, these bat conservation books reflect a broader shift in how bats are represented in popular literature, moving decisively away from Halloween-season stereotypes toward genuine appreciation for animals that pollinate plants, disperse seeds, and consume enormous quantities of agricultural pests nightly. Whether introducing a child to their first bat-loving picture book character or offering seasoned naturalists a comprehensive species reference, this year’s releases make clear that meaningful conservation storytelling can also be genuinely engaging reading, proving that getting curious about bats might be the easiest first step toward protecting them. The post Bat Conservation Books Offer Something for Every Age appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Νωρίς στο σχολείο, ο Gaurav Marathe αγκάλιασε ένα μάντρα Viraja που μεταφράστηκε από έναν δάσκαλο: "Οι άνθρωποι είναι σαν ένα κερί. Αφού καεί το κερί, ο άνθρακας μένει πάνω του, και πρέπει να αφαιρέσετε αυτόν τον μαύρο άνθρακα από το φως, ώστε το φως να ανάψει ξανά." Το μάντρα του έμαθε να πειραματίζεται τόσο με την αφαίρεση του άνθρακα όσο και με το φωτισμό του jyoti -- το φως…
items.descriptionOriginal: Early on in school, Gaurav Marathe embraced a Viraja mantra translated by a teacher: "Humans are like a candle. After the candle burns, carbon stays on it, and you have to remove that black carbon from the light so the light again illuminates." The mantra taught him to experiment with both removing the carbon and illuminating the jyoti -- the light that exists within. In one of many experiments, he challenged students to remove the carbon of a task-driven, rule-driven festival on a campus where he taught. "Let's do that experiment. Let it be the kind of carnival where nobody is charging anything. No cost price, nothing. If anybody wants to pay, they pay. If they don't, they don't. Let's believe in that spirit." It was successful beyond anyone's imagination, and became a "Soul Carnival" where the focus is on giving over profiting. "Perhaps that's the point of these experiments — not to have all the answers, but to keep creating spaces where we can go close to inner jyoti a little more."

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article kicks off The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. It was winter break, and Dilan Mehta had time on his hands. His dad was packing for a mission trip to Kenya, where he’d been volunteering with Kenya Relief , a medical organization that runs a school in Migori, for years. Dilan packed a bag of stuffed animals for the children there. Then he glanced at his 3D printer. He started designing LEGO-inspired sets, printing each one out, and tucking them in alongside the stuffed animals. Somewhere between one print and the next, a different thought took shape. The school had students who could use a curriculum, and his dad had room in a suitcase. That’s how a 3D printer ended up in Migori, Kenya, and why it’s still being used to teach students today. What is Student Makers? Student Makers is a nonprofit that offers free STEM workshops to students across the United States, Kenya, and India, and every instructor is a former student. Most of them are still in high school. The organization was founded in California in 2019 by Anthony Neil Tan, then a high school senior. There was no space at his school where students interested in technology and making could come together to learn, so he built one. He called it the Maker Hub Club Initiative, secured a $5,000 grant from a social impact scholarship, and got it off the ground. The framework was three steps: learn a skill , make a project, showcase it. He was in his first year of college when he started handing it off. Serve: the fourth pillar Dilan didn’t find Student Makers; rather, Anthony found him. Roughly six years ago, Dilan was only in 8th grade and had entered an Autodesk design contest with a 3D-printed fingerboard, one that used flexible filament on the grip surface to behave like rubber. Anthony came across it and reached out. Would Dilan want to join a group where students build things and learn from each other? He joined, took the 3D printing course, came back as an instructor, and eventually rebuilt the entire curriculum from scratch around design thinking rather than output. A few years later, he was running the organization. But he felt that the project’s mission needed some rethinking. The original framework had three steps: learn, make, showcase. Dilan added a fourth, serve, because the workshops were primarily reaching students who already had resources, and that wasn’t what he’d signed up for. His dad’s Kenya-bound suitcase gave him the opening for a bigger idea to launch. Teaching through rain and static When Dilan sent that 3D printer to Kenya Relief Academy, he wasn’t thinking about it as a program. He was thinking about a school with 800 students, roughly 170 to 190 of them orphaned children, consistently ranked the top primary school in its region out of more than 800, and without any STEM infrastructure. His dad’s Kenya Relief contacts connected him to the teachers there, and he started meeting with them remotely three times a week. Every session ran over video call, Dilan in the US and the teachers in Migori, and when the Wi-Fi dropped, which it often would, they’d wait, reconnect, and keep going. He trained them in Autodesk Fusion 360, Tinkercad, and 3D printer operation, working through how to teach all of it to a classroom he’s never seen in person. “They constantly have Wi-Fi issues,” Dilan said. “Anytime there’s rain, they basically lose connection. Just being patient, being empathetic , understanding that that’s just the situation.” Ruth Agongo, a teacher at Kenya Relief Academy, described what it looked like from the other end. “You are a game-changer,” she said. “Whatever you have taught us, we are putting into action because the kids are really excited by the technology.” Jacob A few semesters into his time at Georgia Tech, once Dilan had actually taken a step back from Student Makers and was serving mostly as an advisory board member, Dilan got a message from the teachers at Kenya Relief Academy. They needed help with a science fair project: an Arduino-based robot that could navigate a garden, measure soil moisture at different points, and decide where to water. Dilan didn’t know much about robotics, but he was at Georgia Tech, so he asked around. Twelve students from the university ended up on the project. They built components in Atlanta while the Kenya team built in Migori, troubleshot over video call, and sent physical supplies through a similar suitcase network that had carried the original printer. That team placed third at regionals of the Kenya Science and Engineering Fair. One of the students on it, a ninth-grader named Jacob, now leads Kenya Relief Academy’s robotics team. His dream is to become a rocket engineer at NASA. A family connection in India Rohan Naegle, who led Student Makers before the current team took over, brought a similar program to Dr. R.V. Shah English Medium School in rural Gujarat, India, after his grandfather put him in touch with the school. Live 3D printing classes run there over video call, using the same structure. More than 25 secondary students have completed the program, and a donated printer stays at the school. Both the Kenya and India connections came organically, through family. How the pipeline runs Aarush Goel, who now leads the high school chapters, came in the same way Dilan did: a friend pulled him in to co-teach a Python workshop, and he showed up not entirely sure what he was doing. “You just start teaching and everything goes into place,” he said. He’s since led five workshop tracks across the US, and next year he’ll start a Student Makers chapter at his own college. Instructors are recruited the same way at every level. At the end of each cycle, a call goes out for anyone who wants to come back and teach the next round. Usually one or two students say yes. They already know the program from the inside, which tends to make them good at the part that matters most: building something new students actually want to stay in. Anthony, watching from his current advisory role, put it plainly. “It’s more relatable, a high schooler showing a middle schooler how to do some 3D printing than someone who’s already a young adult,” he said. “So it’s nice keeping that peer-to-peer instruction model.” He’s 25. The organization he started as a high school senior just turned seven. Growing the network Student Makers recently joined a partnership with Youth Technology Corps Global Alliance , a network of schools across roughly 12 countries that has been running a similar peer-learning model since 1998. YTC has been doing this for nearly three decades and has school connections worldwide; Student Makers brings the volunteers and the curriculum. This fall, programs are launching under the partnership in Mexico, Colombia, Ethiopia, and Illinois, with the 3D printing and CAD curriculum going into Mexico specifically. “I would have never imagined that we would have this extensive of a reach,” Anthony said. The reach he couldn’t have imagined started with a simple observation: students interested in technology and making didn’t have a space to come together. So he built one. Why Student Makers opens this year’s series Each year, The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers series runs in the weeks before Thanksgiving, and this year, for the first time, every person in it is 30 or under. When Aarush reached out to us with the Student Makers story last summer, we spent weeks talking with the people who built this organization and were honestly floored by their dedication, hard work, and willingness to serve others. The five other changemakers in this year’s series were nominated by The Optimist Daily community, but Student Makers was not. It was the story that inspired the decision behind this year’s “30 and under” theme. This article skims the surface of the deeper story behind Student Makers. If you want to learn more about their incredible work, hang tight for a podcast episode featuring the voices behind this initiative. It’ll be coming out in early 2027. In the meantime, you can learn more and support their work at www.studentmakers.org . The post Student Makers, a deeper dive: bringing free STEM to students on three continents first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old. ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient. “Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request. Volunteers with the All The Same Organization Reaching Title I families across the country Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season , the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods. ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over. Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.” Cultural Surprises Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for. Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.” Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost. ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.” A classroom, and what came after After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School. When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away. “Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote. Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit. Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org . Vivian Ho, founder. The post Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Πολλές από αυτές τις πόλεις r…
items.descriptionOriginal: From the deep South to colonial New England, certain U.S. locales have developed chilling reputations for reports of apparitions and other paranormal activity. Long shadows have been cast by histories steeped in calamity, and stories abound of restless souls condemned to cemeteries and peevish poltergeists with bones to pick. Many of these cities relish their notoriety, with multiple laying claim to the title of most haunted in the country. We detail a few of them below, but whether you use this list as a roster of places you dare not enter or as a resource for your next vacation, proceed with caution: We can’t promise that reading our roundup won’t summon the spirits mentioned within it. Savannah, Georgia Glen Richard—iStock/Getty Images Plus Savannah offers all the charm of the South and all the unease of a Southern Gothic novel — if you know where to look. Lurking amid the oak-lined streets and majestic mansions are specters borne of centuries of tragedy (or so the story goes). Founded in 1733, the city played major roles in the Revolutionary and Civil Wars and was ravaged by several yellow fever outbreaks in the 1800s. The souls lost in those events are said to haunt Savannah’s historic cemeteries and buildings. “Visitors and locals alike report unexplained phenomena across Savannah: sudden cold spots, shadow figures, voices, apparitions, and objects moving without cause,” claims local hotel Bellwether House, which was built in 1876. “Ghost sightings aren’t confined to one building — they’re woven into the city itself.” Even its own chamber of commerce boasts its reputation as “the most haunted city in America” (a title New Orleans also claims). Check out 10 of the spookiest places in Savannah. Atchison, Kansas DonsESLAdventure—iStock Editorial/Getty Images Plus Known for being the birthplace of Amelia Earhart , Atchison’s other claim to fame is its purported paranormal activity. Situated on the Missouri River, it’s home to the infamous Sallie House . Legend has it that after a young girl named Sallie died there during a failed appendicitis operation in 1905, her ghost stuck around. Though locals had long considered the abode haunted, the story truly took hold in 1993 when a couple moved in and began experiencing ominous phenomena — including a fire, objects moving around on their own, and unexplained scratches. Other eerie sites in Atchison (called “America’s most haunted town” by its tourism department) include the McInteer Villa , an 1889 Victorian mansion that’s elicited reports of supernatural occurrences; the Rose Trunk Building , where visitors have claimed they sensed an unseen presence; and Benedictine College, said to be haunted by the spirits of monks who founded it over 150 years ago. New Orleans, Louisiana lightphoto—iStock/Getty Images Plus Welcome to New Orleans, a 308-year-old city rife with historical trauma. Its early days were marked by violence and sorrow, which continued into the 19th century as slavery, the Civil War, and several disease outbreaks took their toll. A merging of West African spiritual practices and Catholicism gave rise to its distinct voodoo tradition , and today, “the line between the living and the dead often feels surprisingly thin,” per the city’s tourism department. If you’re looking for a hair-raising time, you should certainly visit the French Quarter. Book a stay at the Andrew Jackson Hotel — believed to be haunted by five boys who perished there in a fire when it was a boarding school — or dine at Antoine’s Restaurant, reportedly home to 19th-century spirits who peer out from the bathroom mirrors. The ghost of author William Faulkner is said to remain in the rooms he rented in the neighborhood, which have since been converted into a bookstore called Faulkner House Books. Learn about more haunted places in New Orleans. Salem, Massachusetts AndTheyTravel—iStock Editorial / Getty Images Plus Salem’s dark history has seemingly cast a spell over the colonial New England town. The area’s notorious witch trials saw around 200 people accused of witchcraft in the 1690s. About 30 were found guilty and at least 19 were put to death. Today, this chilling past resurfaces in reports of ghost sightings and other supernatural phenomena. Proctor’s Ledge , the trials’ primary execution site, is said to be haunted, with visitors reporting cold spots, incandescent orbs, and a disembodied voice, per Ghost City Tours. The Joshua Ward House , built on the site where George Corwin — High Sheriff during the witch trials — once lived, is also the stuff of legend: An accused man named Giles Corey is rumored to have cursed Corwin and the town of Salem with his final breath during his execution. At the Old Burying Point Cemetery , established in 1637, condemned souls are believed to be responsible for mysterious shadows, noises, mist, and an overwhelming sense of despair. Anoka, Minnesota Officially known as “the Halloween Capital of the World,” Anoka is rich with tales of the paranormal. Reportedly haunted buildings include the Anoka State Hospital , a psychiatric institution that opened in 1900; Colonial Hall, where furniture is said to move around inexplicably after dark; and the old Anoka library, with a known history of “books flying off of shelves,” per local outlet HometownSource. The Anoka County Historical Society, which formerly used the library as its headquarters, offers guided ghost tours that are “60% history, 40% folklore” and based on real stories from the people who live and work in the city’s buildings. Virginia City, Nevada NNehring—E+/Getty Images “To say everything is haunted in this old mining town is not too far from the truth,” proclaims Virginia City’s tourism department. The locale topped the ranking in the 2026 Spookiest Cities Report , a playful analysis by home security company Vivint. The ranking used seven measures, adjusted for population: haunted places, ghost sightings, funeral services, haunted houses, psychics and astrologers, spiritual shops, and spooky Google search volume. Visitors can explore eerie places like the Gold Hill Hotel, Nevada’s oldest, where rumors persist of children’s ghosts running the halls, or bring home a bottle of Cemetery Gin, the city’s own distilled spirit. This month — dubbed Hauntober — one of the area’s top ghost experts is leading paranormal investigations at the historic St. Mary’s Art Center, which was originally a hospital and is known as one of Virginia City’s most haunted buildings. Gettysburg, Pennsylvania pabradyphoto— iStock/Getty Images Plus The Civil War’s Battle of Gettysburg in 1863 resulted in over 50,000 casualties, and many believe that the spirits of the soldiers who died on the battlefield remain there, reliving the brutal conflict. For over 100 years, visitors and locals have reported “phantom footsteps, ghostly drumbeats, and echoes of musket fire and cannon blasts,” per History . Other spots in the city, widely known as one of the country’s most haunted places , have their own eerie history tied to the war. The Jennie Wade House Museum commemorates, and is said to be possessed by, the only civilian killed in the battle. Visitors have claimed to hear whispers, feel cold spots, and see Wade’s ghost floating through the rooms. Those daring enough to walk into the Sachs Covered Bridge — where a trio of Confederate soldiers were executed for impersonating Union troops — may encounter three disembodied heads or feel phantom fingers tapping their shoulders.
